and RV64 has FOUR, so a call with five arguments spills on one target and not
the other. Every RV64-only bug this session has come from exactly that kind of
asymmetry.

FRAME LAYOUTS ARE IDENTICAL ACROSS TARGETS, which rules out the layout
arithmetic as the remaining cause:

    x86-64  outer%2.2  outgoing=0 spills=5 bytes=64
    rv64    outer%2.2  outgoing=0 spills=5 bytes=64

(and every other function matches too). So frame-slot-offset, the outgoing shift
and the borrow area are all computing the same thing on both targets. The
divergence is in the SPILL REWRITING, not the layout.

WHAT DIFFERS. Writes to the frame in outer%2.2:

    x86-64, 6 writes:  [rsp+0] once, then +8 +16 +24 +16 +32
    rv64,   7 writes:  [sp+0] THREE TIMES, plus +8 +16 +24

The extra writes to slot 0 -- which holds n -- come from load-modify-store
round-trips the rv64 spiller emits:

    (ld t1 sp 0) (addi t0 t1 0) (sd t0 sp 0)

x86-64 has no equivalent because its instructions take memory operands
directly, so a spilled value can be read in place; RV64 is load/store and must
materialise through a register. That is legitimate in principle -- reading a
slot and writing the same value back is a no-op -- and it is where to look,
because it is the only place slot 0 is written after the loop head and the only
structural difference between the two targets here.

NEXT: check what the rv64 spiller actually round-trips through slot 0. If the
register it writes back is not the one it read -- because the borrow register
was reused between the load and the store, which is the hazard borrow-words
exists for -- then n is replaced by something else and the symptom follows
exactly.

STATUS. Three real compiler bugs have come out of this bead so far, each hidden
behind the last: address-into taking #f as an index (1mp.7), the
return-address word in frame-incoming-offset, and own-label? reading RV64s
destination register as a jump target (4142485). The first three iterations of
the loop now run correctly where none did before. This remaining one is
spiller-level and wants a focused sitting rather than another loop tick.

THE REMAINING BUG IS A STACK LEAK, MEASURED. sp at the same instruction on
successive outer iterations:

    0x77ee0ebffd20
    0x77ee0ebffd20
    0x77ee0ebffd60      +0x40
    0x77ee0ebffda0      +0x40

sp climbs by exactly 64 -- outer%2.2 s frame size -- per pass. So a frame is
RELEASED without being RESERVED, and after two passes [sp+0] no longer names
the slot holding n. That is why t3 reads a stack address: not a corrupted
value, a correct load from a stack pointer that has walked away.

THE LISTING LOOKS BALANCED, which is why this needs the binary rather than the
IR:

    outer%2.2:            (addi sp sp -64)     prologue
    outer%2.2.loop:       ...
                          (addi sp sp 64)      epilogue
                          (jal zero outer%2.2) to the ENTRY, which re-pushes

Pop then push: balanced as written. So either the emitted jump does not land on
the entry, or a path reaches an epilogue without having run the prologue.

WHERE TO LOOK. finalize.ss carries an optimisation described at its own comment
"a self tail call jumps PAST the prologue": it rewrites the back edge to the
.loop label and drops the matching epilogue, on the grounds that "both cancel
and both disappear". If that rewrite drops the epilogue but leaves the target at
the entry -- or rewrites the target but leaves the epilogue -- the result is
exactly a frame-sized drift per iteration. It is also precisely the kind of
paired rewrite that an x86-only spelling check would half-apply on RV64, which
is what the last seven bugs on this target have been.

Note this is the SAME hazard that comment was written about, from the other
direction: it warns that treating the back edge as an intra-function edge skips
the epilogue while the prologue still runs, growing the stack DOWNWARD. This is
the mirror -- the epilogue runs and the prologue does not -- so the stack grows
UPWARD instead.

Everything else in the argument path is now correct: setup emits
(addi t4 zero 1) / (addi t5 zero 0) directly, matching x86-64.

ROOT CAUSE FOUND: RV64 NON-LEAF FUNCTIONS DO NOT SAVE `ra`.

Totalling every sp adjustment over a run:

    -64 x1     outer%2.2 prologue      ONCE
    +64 x2     outer%2.2 epilogue      TWICE
    NET +48

One prologue, two epilogues. outer%2.2 is entered once and leaves twice, which
is only possible if it re-enters itself -- and it does:

    outer%2.2 calls inner with   (jal ra inner%5.15)
    outer%2.2 returns with       (jalr zero ra 0)

`jal ra` OVERWRITES ra with the address after the call. So when outer%2.2
returns, it jumps back into its own body just past that call, runs the loop
again, and exits again. sp climbs a frame each time and [sp+0] stops naming the
slot holding n -- which is the "corruption" every earlier diagnosis chased.

WHY x86-64 CANNOT SHOW THIS. `call` PUSHES the return address onto the stack, so
a callee cannot destroy its caller s. On RV64 the return address lives in a
REGISTER, and the ABI requires every non-leaf function to save and restore it.
This compiler never emits that save, because on the target it was written for
there is nothing to save.

That is the same root shape as the other eight RV64 bugs this session -- an
x86-64 assumption that does not survive a load/store target -- but this one is
the ABI rather than an operand spelling, which is why it outlasted them.

THE FIX, and it is real work rather than a spelling change:
  - the frame needs a slot for ra, so frame-layout gains a word on rv64
  - the prologue stores ra into it, the epilogue reloads it, and BOTH only for
    a non-leaf function -- a leaf that saves ra pays for nothing
  - "non-leaf" has to be derived: any function whose listing contains a
    (jal ra ...) or equivalent call
  - every existing sp displacement shifts by that word, which is exactly the
    class of off-by-one-slot the frame diagram warns about, so the incoming
    and slot offsets both need re-checking against it

x86-64 must not gain the slot: its return address is already on the stack and
frame-incoming-offset already steps over it.

EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE RV64 PATH IS NOW CORRECT. Argument setup matches x86-64,
the back edge keeps its frame, the pool addressing resolves, base-only
addressing works, the scratch collision is gone, and a Scheme program runs. This
is the last known blocker for nbody on RV64.
close_reason:
Fixed. The last defect was the RV64 ABI: non-leaf functions never saved `ra`.
x86-64's call PUSHES the return address so a callee cannot destroy its caller's;
RV64's `jal ra` writes a REGISTER, so any function that calls something
overwrites its own return address and `jalr zero ra 0` returns into its own body
just past the call. Measured: outer%2.2 ran its prologue ONCE and its epilogue
TWICE, climbing a frame per pass until [sp+0] no longer named the slot holding the
loop bound -- every earlier diagnosis chased that displaced load as corruption
when it was a correct load from a stack pointer that had walked away.

Non-leaf RV64 functions now save ra outside the spill frame, so no existing
displacement into it moves. The nested-loop reproduction terminates and nbody
runs bit-identically to x86-64 (D81).

Three of my diagnoses on this bead were wrong, each from reading a filtered
artifact rather than the whole one; that is recorded in the notes and in D81
because it cost more than the bug did.

title: RV64 address scratch t0 is clobbered by a constant materialised into the same register
description:
nbody on RV64 segfaults. Single-stepped under qemu to the exact instruction:

    401174:  lui  t0,0x600
    401178:  addi t0,t0,88     # t0 = 0x600058   <- address computed
    40117c:  li   t0,5         # t0 = 5          <- CLOBBERS the address
    401180:  sd   t0,0(t0)     # store 5 to address 5 -> SIGSEGV

(li is objdump aliasing addi t0,zero,5.)

The address is computed into t0, which is rv64-addr-scratch, and then the VALUE
being stored is materialised into t0 as well. The store then uses t0 as both
base and source, writing 5 to address 5.

TWO RULES IN ONE SEQUENCE BOTH CLAIMED THE SAME SCRATCH. target-rv64.ss warns
about this in its own header -- note 1, "the address temporary is a register
selection has no way to ask for, because a rule returns instructions and
nothing else" -- and rv64-addr-scratch is a parameter precisely so the conflict
is visible. This is that conflict actually firing.

NOT A REGISTER-ALLOCATOR BUG. regs.ss keeps t0/t1/t2 out of the allocatable
pools, so the allocator never handed t0 to a virtual. Both uses come from
SELECTION: address-into takes the scratch, and whatever materialised the
constant took it too.

WHERE TO LOOK: the rule that emits the constant into a destination, when that
destination is itself the scratch, or a store rule that computes its address
before its value. The fix is likely to sequence the value BEFORE the address,
or to give the two uses different scratches -- rv64-overflow-scratch already
shows the pattern of naming more than one.

This is the last known blocker for nbody on RV64. Everything else is in: the
runtime, all six externs, the ELF writer, the driver target path, the base-only
addressing fix (1mp.7) and pool addressing (1mp.8).
acceptance_criteria:
nbody compiles to RV64 and runs under qemu-riscv64 producing energies
bit-identical to the x86-64 build and to bench/nbody/SPEC.md.
notes:
EVERY CLAIMANT OF THE SCRATCH, from a sweep of target-rv64.ss. rv64-addr-scratch
is taken by SEVEN rules:

    183  r:const, float case   the auipc of the pool pair
    299  r:load
    318  r:load-at
    326  r:store-at
    355  (a move/convert rule)
    386  (the address-of helper caller)
    410  r:gref
    415  r:gset

Any two of these firing in one sequence collide. The faulting case pairs the
global-address computation in r:gset with a constant materialised into the same
register.

NOT AN ALLOCATOR BUG, confirmed: regs.ss keeps t0/t1/t2 out of all three rv64
pools -- value is (a0..a7 s2..s7), raw is (s8..s11 t3..t6), and t0/t1/t2 are the
scratch set. The allocator cannot have handed t0 to a virtual, so both writes
come from selection hardcoding the parameter.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT, and it is the one the file header already makes: a rule
returns instructions and nothing else, so it has no way to ASK for a temporary.
Every rule therefore reaches for the same fixed register. That is fine while
only one rule per sequence needs one and breaks the moment two do -- which is
what happens as soon as real IR is selected rather than hand-written fixtures.

So the fix is probably not "use a different register here" but giving selection
a way to request a scratch, or making the sequence explicit about ordering.
rv64-overflow-scratch already names a PAIR, which is the same problem solved
locally once before.

SHARPER DIAGNOSIS from a wider disassembly window. My first reading -- "two
selection rules both take the scratch" -- is not what the code shows.

FLOAT global stores are FINE, and the contrast is the clue:

    401160:  auipc t0,0x2        ; float const: t0 is the auipc base
    401164:  fld   ft1,-1624(t0)
    401168:  lui   t0,0x600      ; gset address, t0 reused -- safe, ft1 holds the value
    40116c:  addi  t0,t0,72
    401170:  fsd   ft1,0(t0)

The value lives in a FLOAT register, so reusing t0 for the address costs
nothing. The integer case has nowhere else to put the value:

    401174:  lui   t0,0x600      ; gset address into t0
    401178:  addi  t0,t0,88
    40117c:  addi  t0,zero,5     ; the VALUE, into the same register
    401180:  sd    t0,0(t0)

AND CONSTANTS ARE BEING STAGED THROUGH t0 GENERALLY, which is the part I had
wrong. Twenty bytes later:

    401190:  addi  t0,zero,15
    401194:  addi  t3,t0,0       ; move to the real register

So a constant is materialised into t0 and then moved out. r:const does NOT do
this -- it writes `dst` directly in every arm. So `dst` IS t0 at selection
time, for a virtual the allocator should never have placed there: regs.ss keeps
t0/t1/t2 out of all three rv64 pools.

WHERE TO LOOK NEXT, and it is no longer the selector: something between
selection and encoding is assigning or rewriting into the scratch. Candidates
are the two-address fixup and the parallel-copy break, both of which legitimately
need a temporary and would reach for arch-scratch -- whose first entry is t0,
the same register the address rules take.

That makes this the SAME root cause as the header note after all, but one level
up: two mechanisms need a scratch, both take the first one, and nothing
arbitrates. A fix that merely moves global addressing to t1 would hide this
specific pair and leave the next one.

ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED. It was not two selection rules -- it was selection
against TWOADDR. twoaddr.ss carries its own scratch table:

    (define scratch-table
      (quote ((x86-64 (raw-word . rax) (raw-f64 . xmm15))
              (rv64   (raw-word . t0)  (raw-f64 . ft11)))))

so the two-address fixup stages through t0, and rv64-addr-scratch named t0 too.
Both were drawing legitimately from the three registers regs.ss reserves; both
took the first; nothing arbitrated.

Fixed by moving addressing to t1. Verified: the specific collision is gone and
nbody now faults ~5KB further into the program.

THE GENERAL PROBLEM IS NOT FIXED and should stay open or be re-filed. There are
now three independent consumers of a three-register reserved set --
rv64-addr-scratch (t1), twoaddr raw-word (t0), and rv64-overflow-scratch, which
names a PAIR -- and they coordinate by having been chosen not to overlap rather
than by any mechanism. A fourth consumer, or an overflow check inside an
addressing sequence, reproduces this exactly.

Worth noting twoaddr.ss anticipated half of it: "regs.ss is the source of truth
for WHICH registers are reserved; this table only says which reserved register
serves which storage class, and it is checked against regs.ss on every lookup."
The check confirms the register IS reserved. Nothing checks that two consumers
did not pick the SAME reserved one.

THE GENERAL FORM IS THE REMAINING RV64 BUG, and it is bigger than this bead
first described. Measured, every consumer of the three reserved integer
scratches:

    reserved            (t0 t1 t2 ft9 ft10 ft11)
    spiller integer     (t0 t1 t2)      -- claims ALL THREE
    twoaddr raw-word    t0
    selection address   t1
    selection overflow  (t0 t1)
    argument staging    t0              -- found by the parcopy guard

FIVE consumers, three registers. The spiller is the one that makes it fatal: it
reloads an operand BEFORE an instruction and spills AFTER it, so its register
must survive that instruction s own expansion -- and selection uses t0/t1
INSIDE that expansion. A value reloaded into t1 is destroyed by the address
computation of the very instruction it was reloaded for. That is the remaining
corruption in 1mp.10.

TWO PARTITIONS TRIED, BOTH REFUSED BY AN EXISTING GUARD, which is the useful
result. parcopy raises "argument setup has spill code on the copy own
registers" and it fired on both attempts:

    spiller on (t0 t1 t2), selection moved to s9/s10/s11
        -> (addi t3 t0 0)   argument staging still uses t0
    spiller moved to (s9 s10 s11), selection kept t0-t2
        -> (addi t3 s9 0)   argument setup needs a spill temp of its own

So argument setup both STAGES through a scratch and may itself need a RELOAD,
and those two cannot be the same register. Enlarging the reserved set is not
enough on its own; the argument-setup path needs a register that is neither
selection s staging register nor the spiller s.

Both experiments reverted -- the tree is back to the known state and green.
Recording rather than leaving a partial partition in place, because a scratch
assignment that trips a guard on some programs and not others is worse than the
current single known bug.

WHAT THE FIX PROBABLY IS: give the parallel copy for argument setup its own
reserved register, so the four roles are spiller / selection-internal /
twoaddr / argument-staging and no two overlap. RV64 has room -- the raw pool is
eight registers and s8-s11 are callee-saved allocatables -- but the count has
to be derived from the guard s invariant rather than guessed, which is why this
wants a sitting rather than another loop tick.

THE GUARD IS THE ASSET HERE. It refused both wrong answers immediately and by
name. Whoever takes this should start by reading what it actually requires.

THE GUARD S INVARIANT, READ RATHER THAN GUESSED, and it changes the fix.

finalize.ss resolve-argcopy: within a bracketed argument-copy region, the
`mov-of` instructions ARE the copy; anything else is spill code inserted for
one of them. Spill code may be lifted over the copy ONLY if it does not touch
the copy s registers -- "true for a reload, which reads a frame slot and writes
a SCRATCH, and the scratch classes are outside every pool mov-of admits".

And `mov-of` enforces exactly that by REFUSING a move whose source is a
scratch:

    ((addi) (and ... (not (scratchy? (cadr i))) (not (scratchy? (caddr i)))
                 (cons (cadr i) (caddr i))))

So `(addi t3 t0 0)` is not a copy move -- it is a move OUT OF a scratch, which
by this design means spill code -- and it touches t3, a copy register. The
guard is right to refuse it.

THE ASYMMETRY IS REMATERIALISATION, NOT REGISTER COUNT. Both targets rematerialise
a constant argument rather than spilling and reloading it. x86-64 puts it
STRAIGHT INTO THE ARGUMENT REGISTER:

    (mov rdx (imm 1))

RV64 cannot -- its move is `addi rd, rs, 0`, which has no immediate form -- so
it materialises into a scratch and copies:

    (addi t0 zero 1)
    (addi t4 t0 0)

and that second instruction is a move out of a scratch, which is what the
design reserves for spill code.

SO THE FIX IS NOT MORE SCRATCH REGISTERS. It is to let RV64 rematerialise
directly into the destination. The spiller already has the machinery -- its
remat lambda is (lambda (r d sc) `((addi ,r zero ,d))) and takes the target
register r -- so the question is why the destination is a scratch rather than
the argument register at that point. That is a much smaller change than
partitioning five consumers across three registers, and it explains why both
partitions failed: the register count was never the problem.

I twice tried to fix this by moving registers around. The guard refused both,
by name, immediately. Reading what it required took one command and pointed
somewhere else entirely.

FIXED ONE LAYER: fold-reload is target-agnostic now (committed). RV64
rematerialises a constant argument directly into its destination --
(addi t4 zero 1) -- where it previously staged through a scratch and then moved
out of it, which resolve-argcopy correctly reads as spill code.

REMAINING, and it is a design question rather than a bug hunt. The guard still
fires:

    argument setup has spill code on the copy own registers   (addi t4 zero 1)

because a direct materialisation is not a `mov-of` -- mov-of requires the addi
immediate to be 0, i.e. a register move -- so it lands in `others` and is
flagged for touching t4, a copy register.

On x86-64 the same shape exists, `(mov rdx (imm 1))`, and does NOT trip the
guard: mov-of rejects it too, but rdx is then in `touched` only if some MOVE
reads or writes it, and on x86 nothing else does. On RV64 something in the copy
does touch t4, which is what makes the regions differ.

THE QUESTION: should resolve-argcopy treat a materialisation whose destination
IS a copy register as part of the copy rather than as spill code? It is not
spill code -- it computes an argument, it reads no frame slot, and it is
exactly what the x86 path emits. If so, mov-of or the region classifier needs to
admit "writes a copy destination from no register at all", which is a third
category beside move and spill.

That is a real design call about an invariant this compiler leans on, and the
guard will validate any answer immediately -- it has now refused three wrong
ones by name.

TRIED THE THIRD CATEGORY, AND IT NEEDS MORE THAN mov-of. Making mov-of admit a
materialisation as a copy operation with no source -- (cons dst #f) -- is the
right IDEA and does not work as a one-line change:

    Exception in encode-instr: not an RV64 integer register (#f)
                               in instruction (addi t4 #f 0)

because resolve-moves-in-block does not reorder the original instructions. It
REBUILDS each move from the (dst . src) pair through `emit-mov`, so a source of
#f is emitted literally. A sourceless copy operation would need emit-mov to
carry the original instruction, or to know the immediate.

The other obvious shape -- leave materialisations in `others` and merely exempt
them from the tangled check -- is wrong for a subtler reason: `others` are
emitted BEFORE the resolved copy, so a materialisation into t4 would run before
a move that wanted to READ t4s old value. The tangle check is what currently
prevents that, so exempting it trades a loud error for a silent one.

SO THE HONEST SHAPE OF THE FIX: resolve-moves-in-block has to carry
instructions, not just (dst . src) pairs, so that a copy operation can be
emitted as written rather than reconstructed. That is a change to the parallel
copy s representation and affects both targets.

Reverted; the tree is green at 8571 with the fold-reload fix from the previous
commit, which is a real improvement and stands on its own -- RV64 now
rematerialises directly into the argument register rather than through a
scratch.

Three attempts on this bead have now been refused by the same guard, each for a
different and correct reason. It is doing its job precisely.
close_reason:
Fixed in 4d01cdb, guarded in d0656d9. Root cause was selection against TWOADDR,
not two selection rules: twoaddr.ss carries its own scratch table -- (rv64
(raw-word . t0) (raw-f64 . ft11)) -- so two-address fixups stage through t0, and
rv64-addr-scratch named t0 as well. Both drew legitimately from the three
registers regs.ss reserves; both took the first; nothing arbitrated. The float
path never showed it because a float value lives in an f-register, so reusing t0
for the address is free -- every float global store in the same function was
correct.

Addressing moved to t1, and rv64-test.ss now asserts the two are distinct.
Verified the guard fails on the real collision rather than passing vacuously:
parameterizing rv64-addr-scratch back onto twoaddr's register makes the
predicate #f.

The GENERAL form is pinned rather than fixed, deliberately: rv64-overflow-scratch
names a PAIR and still overlaps both others -- four register-demands against
three integer scratches -- held apart only by an unenforced assumption that
overflow checks compute no addresses. The test asserts that overlap EXISTS, so
the day someone resolves it the test fails and points at the note instead of
passing silently. twoaddr.ss already verifies each register IS reserved; nothing
verifies uniqueness, and that is the gap worth naming.

title: RV64 float constants need a linker: auipc/fld relocations are never applied to a static image
description:
nbody compiles for RV64 and segfaults under qemu-riscv64. The cause is
precise and structural.

    0x401110:  auipc t0,272      # 0x511110
    0x401114:  fld   ft0,272(t0)

auipc shifts its immediate left by 12, so 272 means +1,114,112 bytes, while the
literal pool sits about 272 bytes away. The byte offset has been placed in the
high-20 field without being hi/lo split.

That is not an arithmetic slip. target-rv64.ss r:const says so itself: "The
immediates are the pool offset; THE LINKER overwrites both via the
relocations", and reloc.ss duly builds R_RISCV_PCREL_HI20 and
R_RISCV_PCREL_LO12_I for the pair. The RV64 float-constant path is written for
a linker.

build-executable in elfexec.ss is NOT a linker. It writes a static image by
concatenating code, pool and metadata, and applies no relocations. So the
placeholder immediates reach the running program unchanged and the load goes
wild.

WHY x86-64 NEVER MEETS THIS: its const rule is RIP-relative and resolve-labels
resolves it directly through %pool+N labels -- a scan of a compiled nbody
listing shows dozens of them. No relocation machinery is involved in the
executable path at all.

TWO WAYS OUT:
  (a) apply the two relocations at image-build time, which puts a small linker
      inside elfexec.ss;
  (b) emit the auipc/fld pair against %pool+N labels the way x86-64 does, and
      resolve them in resolve-labels with the hi/lo split.

(b) matches how this tree already works, needs no relocation machinery in the
executable writer, and keeps one mechanism for pool addressing across targets.
The object path can keep its relocations for the case where there IS a linker.
acceptance_criteria:
nbody compiles to RV64 and runs under qemu-riscv64 producing energies
bit-identical to the x86-64 build and to bench/nbody/SPEC.md -- the same oracle
the x86-64 target is held to.
notes:
FIXED, and verified at the instruction level. r:const now emits the pair
against the pool LABEL -- (auipc t (pcrel-hi %pool+N)) / (fld dst t (pcrel-lo
%pool+N)) -- and object.ss resolves both in resolve-labels with the standard
hi/lo split. Option (b) from the description: one mechanism for pool addressing
across both targets, and no relocation machinery in the executable writer. The
object path keeps its relocations for the case where there IS a linker.

pcrel-lo names the SAME label as pcrel-hi rather than carrying its own
displacement, because RISC-V computes the low half relative to the AUIPC pc.
That is exactly why the real R_RISCV_PCREL_LO12_I names the HI20 label instead
of the symbol. The resolver takes the auipc pc as (pc - 4), which holds because
r:const emits the two adjacently and RV64 instructions are all four bytes.

Verified: before, auipc t0,272 meant +1,114,112 bytes with the pool 272 away.
Now:

    401110:  auipc t0,0x2        -> 0x403110
    401114:  fld   ft0,-1520(t0) -> 0x402b20

and the R+X segment runs to 0x402b59, so the load is in range and correct.

A test pinned the old shape and failed, which is right: it asserted the
immediates were NUMBERS, i.e. the linker-dependent form. Updated to assert the
label-relative one.

NBODY STILL SEGFAULTS, on a different and unrelated bug -- filed separately.
This bead is done.
close_reason:
Fixed: r:const emits the auipc/fld pair against the pool label and
resolve-labels performs the hi/lo split, so the static image needs no
relocations. Verified at the instruction level -- the load now lands at 0x402b20
inside the R+X segment where it previously computed +1.1MB out of range. nbody's
remaining segfault is a separate scratch-register collision, filed as its own
bead.

title: RV64 backend emits an instruction with #f where a register belongs
description:
Found by compiling nbody to RV64 for the first time. With the runtime and
externs written, nbody now gets PAST label resolution and fails in encoding:

    not an RV64 integer register (#f)

Something in selection, allocation or finalization produces an rv64
instruction carrying #f in an operand position the encoder reads as a GPR. The
encoder is right to refuse it.

WHY IT WAS NEVER SEEN. D75 recorded that RV64 was verified as an ENCODER and
never as a COMPILATION TARGET: rv64-test.ss and the smoke gate both drive
assemble-function with HAND-WRITTEN instruction bodies, which by construction
contain no #f. No Scheme program had ever been lowered to rv64, so no pass in
the middle had ever produced rv64 output on real IR. This is the first defect
that gap was hiding, and finding one immediately is evidence the gap was
worth closing rather than papering over.

Not diagnosed further. The next step is to walk the finalized rv64 listings
for nbody and find which instruction carries the #f, which localises it to a
pass -- the same per-item approach that found the counter bug in D72.

NOT A BLOCKER FOR THE RUNTIME WORK. The runtime, the externs, the ELF writer
and the driver target path are all in and tested; a trivial Scheme program
compiles to rv64 and runs under qemu. This is the next thing in the way of
nbody specifically.
acceptance_criteria:
nbody compiles to RV64 without error, and the emitted binary runs under
qemu-riscv64 producing energies bit-identical to the x86-64 build and to
bench/nbody/SPEC.md. That is the same oracle the x86-64 target is held to --
no weaker standard for the second target.
notes:
DIAGNOSED AND FIXED, and it uncovered the next blocker.

THE #f: address-into in target-rv64.ss put the index straight into `slli`, so
a BASE-ONLY memory access emitted (slli t0 #f 3). An absent index is spelled #f
everywhere in this tree -- x86-64 writes (mem base #f 1 disp) and its encoder
omits the SIB index. Fixed: no index emits a move instead of a shift-and-add,
so callers keep loading from the scratch with their own displacement.

It survived because rv64-test.ss and the smoke gate drive assemble-function
with HAND-WRITTEN bodies, which by construction contain no #f. Same shape as
the note already in that file about the lowered store surviving "because the
RV64 selector died on the call sequence first". Each gap hides the next.

ALSO FIXED, separately: the encoder raised "not an RV64 integer register (#f)"
naming the operand and not the instruction, which in a compile of any size is a
needle and no haystack. encode-instr now re-raises with the whole instruction
attached. That is what turned this from a search into a one-line answer.

WITH BOTH IN, nbody COMPILES for rv64 -- selection, allocation, encoding,
object emission, the runtime, all six externs. It does not RUN: segfault under
qemu-riscv64, and the cause is precise:

    0x401110:  auipc t0,272      # 0x511110
    0x401114:  fld   ft0,272(t0)

auipc shifts its immediate left by 12, so 272 means +1,114,112 bytes while the
pool is ~272 bytes away. The byte offset is in the high-20 field unsplit.

NOT AN ARITHMETIC SLIP -- it is structural, and target-rv64.ss says so in its
own comment: "The immediates are the pool offset; THE LINKER overwrites both
via the relocations". The RV64 float-constant path is written for a LINKER, and
reloc.ss duly builds R_RISCV_PCREL_HI20 and R_RISCV_PCREL_LO12_I. But
build-executable is a static image writer -- it concatenates code and pool and
applies no relocations at all. So the placeholders survive into the image.

x86-64 never meets this because its const rule is RIP-relative and
resolve-labels handles it directly through %pool+N labels, which is why the
label scan earlier showed dozens of them.

SO THE REMAINING WORK IS PC-RELATIVE POOL ADDRESSING FOR RV64 IN THE STATIC
IMAGE PATH: either apply the two relocations at image-build time, or emit the
pair against %pool+N labels the way x86-64 does and resolve them in
resolve-labels. The second matches how this tree already works and needs no
relocation machinery in the executable writer.

Filed separately so 1mp.6 is not blocked on it: the runtime, externs, ELF
writer, driver target and this #f fix are all in and tested.
close_reason:
Fixed in b78dbfe. address-into in target-rv64.ss put the index straight into
slli, so a BASE-ONLY memory access emitted (slli t0 #f 3). An absent index is
spelled #f everywhere in this tree -- x86-64 writes (mem base #f 1 disp) and its
encoder omits the SIB index. No index now emits a move rather than a
shift-and-add, so callers keep loading from the scratch with their own
displacement.

It survived because rv64-test.ss and the smoke gate drive assemble-function with
hand-written bodies, which by construction contain no #f -- the same shape as the
note in that file about the lowered store surviving because the selector died on
the call sequence first.

Also fixed alongside: encode-instr now re-raises with the whole instruction
attached, where it previously named only the offending operand. That is what
turned the search into a one-line answer, and it is why the two bugs after this
one took minutes rather than hours.

title: The driver has no RV64 target path: compile-sonic hardcodes x86-64 at every stage
description:
Found while checking whether M4 (qaq.6) could be closed. Its acceptance is
"packed arithmetic verified in disassembly on x86-64 AND RV64", and the RV64
half is blocked by something no bead tracks.

THERE IS NO WAY TO COMPILE A SCHEME PROGRAM TO RV64. driver.ss exports exactly
two entry points and neither takes a target:

    (define (compile-sonic path externs))
    (define (compile-sonic-to-file path externs out))

The symbol x86-64 is hardcoded at every stage inside them -- select-program
x86-64-selector, finalize-program with arch-x86-64, runtime-listing x86-64,
assemble-function x86-64, build-executable x86-64, instruction-size x86-64.
The string rv64 does not appear in driver.ss at all.

WHAT RV64 SUPPORT ACTUALLY IS. Real, and at the wrong level for this. The
symbol rv64 appears in target-rv64.ss, regs.ss, finalize.ss, object.ss,
gcmeta.ss and vec-rv64.ss -- encoder, register file, frame layout, object
emission. It is exercised by rv64-test.ss and by harness/smoke-riscv.sh, and
the smoke gate reads our own output back through riscv64-linux-gnu-objdump,
which is a real check. But the gate assembles a HAND-WRITTEN instruction body:

    (function-object-elf (assemble-function (quote rv64) (quote sonic_nbody_inner) body))

That is the assembler being driven directly, not a program going through the
pipeline. So RV64 is verified as an ENCODER and never as a COMPILATION TARGET.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND M4. Every claim of the form "tested on both targets"
means "the back-end machinery is tested on both targets". No Scheme program
has ever been compiled to RV64 by this compiler. That is not a defect in the
RV64 code -- what exists looks sound -- it is a gap between what the tests
establish and what the milestones read as.

AND slp PACKING IS x86-ONLY, separately. slp-program runs unconditionally at
driver.ss:145, but its packed operations have lowerings in target-x86-64.ss
and none in target-rv64.ss:

    p2add   x86-64:1   rv64:0
    p2sub   x86-64:1   rv64:0
    p2mul   x86-64:1   rv64:0
    p2div   x86-64:1   rv64:0

So even with a driver target path, packed arithmetic on RV64 needs a lowering
that does not exist -- either these pairs onto RVV, or the vectorize.ss route.
acceptance_criteria:
Either a Scheme program compiles end to end to RV64 and its disassembly is
asserted the way the x86-64 path already is; or the scope is stated explicitly
-- RV64 is an encoder target, not a compilation target -- and every milestone
saying "both targets" is reworded to match what is actually verified.
notes:
SIZED, and it is much smaller than the bead description implies. Most of an
RV64 compilation path already exists and is tested.

PRESENT AND TESTED:
    rv64-selector      target-rv64.ss:587, (make-selector rv64 rv64-rules
                       arch-rv64) -- a full 588-line backend with FMA rules,
                       call emitter, trap label, litpool
    arch-rv64          regs.ss
    finalize           7 rv64 mentions
    object emission    21 rv64 mentions
    litpool            handled

MISSING, and both refuse LOUDLY rather than silently, which is why none of
this was a live hazard:
    runtime listing    runtime.ss:858 refuses for rv64. This is the entry
                       point, argv handling, output, exit -- the RISC-V
                       syscall ABI.
    runnable image     elfexec.ss build-executable/meta refuses non-x86-64,
                       and e_machine is hardcoded EM_X86_64 (0x3e). RV64
                       needs EM_RISCV (0xf3).
    driver plumbing    compile-sonic takes no target argument, so the two
                       refusals above are not even reachable through it.

THE ARGUMENT AGAINST DOING IT HAS EXPIRED. runtime.ss justified its refusal
with "an RV64 one written blind would be validated by nothing". That was true
when written and is not true now: THE CONTAINER HAS qemu-riscv64 10.1.0.
Verified end to end -- riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc builds a static binary,
qemu-riscv64 runs it, prints the right answer. So an RV64 runtime can be
validated exactly the way the x86-64 one is: emit it, run it, compare the
energies against SPEC.md. That is the same standard, not a weaker one.

The premise expired because the container gained qemu for instruction counting
and nobody revisited a comment that depended on its absence. Same shape as
vec-x86-64.ss header (D74): a true statement falsified by an unrelated change,
with nothing to notice. Both refusal messages corrected (D76) -- they still
refuse, they just no longer claim the work is unverifiable.

SO THE DECISION IS BETTER POSED NOW: this is a bounded piece of work with all
the hard parts already done and a real validation route, not an open-ended
port. It is still not the loop calling: writing a runtime entry sequence and
an ELF image writer for a second architecture is a feature, and which target
this project spends time on is a priorities question.

Note the smoke gate remains a genuine check of what it covers -- it reads our
own rv64 output back through riscv64-linux-gnu-objdump. It just covers the
encoder, on a hand-written body, not the pipeline.

CORRECTING MY OWN SIZING. The note above says the missing work is "bounded" and
that "all the hard parts already exist". That was measured wrong -- I counted
what EXISTS (rv64-selector, arch-rv64, encoder, object emission) and inferred
the remainder was small, without measuring the remainder. Measured now:

    x86-64-listing        689 lines
                          289 emitted instructions
                           39 helper routines

Those helpers are not translations of compiler output. They are hand-written
runtime, and an RV64 version has to REPRODUCE the behaviour rather than port
the encoding:

    allocation          5 labels  %make-flvector %make-vector %cons %c2s-alloc ...
    boxing / tagging    5         %box-flonum %fixnum %flonum %pair %null
    string conversion   7         %cstr->string %s2n-* %c2s-*
    integer division    3         %fxquotient %fxremainder %fxmodulo
    error / trap        1         %error

Plus entry, heap pointer and gcmeta setup, the command-line list walk, and the
exit path. Different register conventions, different addressing modes, a
different syscall ABI, and RISC-V has no direct equivalent for several of the
x86 addressing forms these rely on.

So this is a FEATURE, not a gap to be tidied: several hundred lines of new
hand-written runtime for a second architecture, plus the EM_RISCV image writer
and the driver target argument. The earlier "bounded" framing should not be
used to decide it.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE. The validation route is still real -- qemu-riscv64 10.1.0
is in the container, so the result can be run and checked against SPEC.md
exactly as the x86-64 runtime is. D76 stands: the reason recorded in
runtime.ss for not doing it ("would be validated by nothing") is expired. It is
worth doing on its merits. It is just considerably more work than I said.

I am not starting it inside a loop iteration. Not because it is out of bounds
-- LOOP.md puts "implement beads that are ready" under DO FREELY -- but because
several hundred lines of hand-written runtime for an architecture, landed
piecemeal across cron firings, is how you get a half-ported runtime that
compiles and produces wrong numbers. It wants one deliberate sitting with the
oracle as the gate.

STARTED. First increment landed: the RV64 encoder now has ecall.

It was ABSENT, and that is a prerequisite my sizing missed twice -- both times
by counting what exists rather than testing what a runtime actually needs.
Linux/RV64 puts the syscall number in a7 and arguments in a0-a5, so without
ecall an emitted program can neither write output nor exit. No runtime of any
kind was possible before this.

SYSTEM opcode 0b1110011, all fields zero, fixed word 0x00000073. Verified
byte-for-byte against riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc, per the rule in encode-rv64.ss
header that correctness is DEFINED as agreement with binutils.

THE COVERAGE GUARD FIRED, which is worth recording because it is the habit
LOOP.md recommends. rv64-test.ss asserts that the differential listing covers
every mnemonic the encoder knows, so adding ecall to instr-table without adding
it to the cross-checked listing failed the suite immediately -- 43 checks, 1
failure. I confirmed that failure BEFORE satisfying it. An encoder entry that
is never compared against the assembler is exactly the shape of bug this
project keeps finding.

REMAINING, unchanged in scope:
    runtime listing   689 lines, 289 instructions, 39 helpers to reproduce
    runnable image    EM_RISCV in elfexec.ss (e_machine is hardcoded 0x3e)
    driver plumbing   a target argument on compile-sonic

The runtime is the bulk and still wants one deliberate sitting with the oracle
as the gate, rather than being accreted across cron firings. But the
prerequisite is real and is now in, byte-verified.

THIRD INCREMENT. The driver takes a target now, and nbody reaches the RV64
runtime boundary.

compile-sonic/compile-sonic-to-file take an optional target defaulting to
x86-64. It had been hardcoded at seven sites, which is why RV64 could not even
be REQUESTED.

Requesting it exposed a FOURTH missing piece -- the third time sizing this by
inspection has under-counted, and the first time the request itself told me:

    target cannot select these ops (rv64 (p2splat p2mul p2add p2sub p2hi))

slp.ss packs unconditionally and only target-x86-64.ss lowers a packed pair.
Gated slp on target; RV64 gets correct scalar code. Noted in the code that this
should become a capability test rather than a target-name test once RV64 has any
packed lowering.

STATUS NOW:
    encoder        ecall added, byte-verified against binutils
    ELF image      EM_RISCV, e_flags 0x4, RUNS under qemu (exit-42 asserted)
    driver         takes a target; slp gated
    selection      handles real nbody on rv64
    allocation     handles real nbody on rv64
    encoding       handles real nbody on rv64
    object         handles real nbody on rv64
    RUNTIME        <- the only remaining gap

That is a much stronger position than this bead started in: everything except
the runtime listing is now demonstrated on a REAL program rather than a
hand-written fixture, which is exactly the gap D75 said the "both targets"
claims were papering over.

The new test pins the BOUNDARY rather than a capability. Compiling nbody for
rv64 must fail and must fail AT THE RUNTIME; a test asserting merely "rv64
fails" would have passed the whole time it was dying in selection.

Remaining: the runtime listing. 689 lines, 39 helpers, to be reproduced against
a different register convention, addressing modes and syscall ABI. Still wants
one deliberate sitting with the oracle as the gate.

NBODY NOW RUNS 564,840,024 INSTRUCTIONS on RV64 before faulting -- it is
executing the simulation, not dying at startup.

Two more of my own bugs found and fixed since the last note:

  RETURN REGISTER. %make-flvector returned in t3. The COUNT arrives in t3
  because it is a raw word, but the RESULT is a tagged heap pointer and
  callconv-rv64 returns those in a0. I took the register from the argument
  class rather than the result class. x86-64 hides the distinction by using
  rax for both, so reading across from it cannot catch this.

  It failed silently and far from its cause: the caller stored a0 -- holding
  whatever it held -- into the flvector global, so every later element store
  addressed off null and the crash appeared thousands of bytes away looking
  like a bad index.

  SCRATCH COLLISION (1mp.9). Addressing and twoaddr both took t0.

REMAINING FAULT, and it is not mine this time:

    401268:  add  t1,a0,t1
    40126c:  fld  ft1,7(t1)

+7 is (8 - heap-tag), the CDR offset. An flvector ELEMENT wants
heap-element-disp = -1, which rv64-test.ss pins for r:load. So a different rule
-- r:load-at takes its own offset argument -- is computing a pair displacement
where it wants an element one. Reads one element past.

That the program gets half a billion instructions in before hitting it suggests
it is a rarer path rather than the main loop.

CORRECTION, AND IT CHANGES THE DIAGNOSIS. The +7 displacement is NOT a bug. I
read it as the cdr offset; it is offset-disp for a constant element offset:

    (define (offset-disp who d) (+ heap-element-disp (* d 8)))

so d=1 gives -1 + 8 = 7, which reaches the NEXT element -- the y component from
an x index. Correct arithmetic, correctly folded into RV64 single addressing
mode. r:load uses heap-element-disp = -1 for a bare element; r:load-at folds
the constant offset in. Both right.

THE ACTUAL SIGNAL IS THE INSTRUCTION COUNT. nbody at N=1000 retires about
664,000 instructions on x86-64 -- 664 per step, measured, times 1000 steps. The
RV64 build executed 564,840,024 before faulting. That is ~850x too many.

So the program is NOT progressing through the simulation and crashing at the
end. It is LOOPING, and the fault is what finally happens when an index walks
off the array. The bad displacement I went looking for was a symptom of an
index that should never have reached that value.

WHERE TO LOOK: loop control on RV64. RISC-V has no flags register --
target-rv64.ss note 2 -- so every comparison is materialised into a register
and branched on separately, via slt/xori for the ordering cases. A comparison
whose sense is inverted, or a branch reading the wrong sense, produces exactly
this: a loop that runs but never exits. r:cmp-le and r:cmp-ge are the suspects
worth reading first, since both are a slt followed by an xori to negate, and
that negation is the easiest thing to get backwards.

The x86-64 build of the same source is bit-exact against SPEC.md, so this is
target-specific rather than a compiler-wide fault.

NOTE THE MEASUREMENT WAS AVAILABLE ALL ALONG and I did not use it: the whole
project has an instruments harness that reports instructions per step, and one
comparison against the x86-64 number would have said "this is looping" before I
disassembled anything.

COMPARISON RULES RULED OUT, which was my stated prime suspect. Read them
directly:

    cmp-lt   slt d a b                      a<b
    cmp-gt   slt d b a                      a>b   (operands swapped)
    cmp-le   slt d b a; xori d d 1          not(b<a) = a<=b
    cmp-ge   slt d a b; xori d d 1          not(a<b) = a>=b

All four correct. The float cases use flt.d/fle.d with the operands SWAPPED
rather than the result negated, and target-rv64.ss explains why: those are
quiet-NaN-signalling ordered comparisons giving 0 for any NaN operand, so
swapping yields a correct > and >= while negating would yield 1 for NaN. That
reasoning is right.

    branch-if   (bne cond zero TRUE) (jal zero FALSE)

also correct.

So the non-termination is not in comparison or branch selection. Remaining
candidates, unexamined:
  - the self-tail-call loop form. disasm.ss already knows this compiler emits
    loops as unconditional backward branches, so the loop latch is not a
    conditional branch and the exit test is separate.
  - the induction variable update, particularly whether a fixnum is being
    incremented in its TAGGED or RAW form -- repr.ss is explicit that mixing
    those is a live class of bug, and it is exactly the kind that leaves a
    counter that never reaches its bound.
  - argument passing on the self-call, since a loop whose counter is passed in
    the wrong register would re-enter with the original value forever.

The third is worth checking first: it is target-specific, this is a
target-specific failure, and callconv-rv64 differs from x86-64 in exactly the
place I already got wrong once today (raw-word vs tagged registers).

LOOP INVENTORY, toward the non-termination. The emitted rv64 nbody has 18
backward `jal zero` latches -- this compiler emits loops as unconditional
backward branches, which disasm.ss already documents.

Two are 16 bytes and are MINE, both in the runtime:

    0x401084 -> 0x401074   %mkfl-loop   the flvector fill
    0x4010e4 -> 0x4010d4   %rv-len-loop the length walk

Both re-read and both terminate by construction:

    %mkfl-loop   t2 counts up from 0, t3 holds the count, (bge t2 t3 done)
    %rv-len-loop t0 walks cdrs, exits on (beq t0 sonic-null)

and `length` is called with a0 = nil, so it takes the exit on the first
comparison and returns 0 -- which is what makes nbody take its default N of
1000. So the runtime loops are not the spinning one.

The remaining 16 are the compiled loops, 192 to 820 bytes each, which is the
shape of nbody unrolled bodies.

STILL RUNNING: a hot-pc histogram over the 564M-instruction trace, to say WHICH
latch spins. That is the next concrete step and it needs no guesswork -- the
trace already exists, it is only large.

Reiterating the cheap check I skipped and should not have: the instruments
harness reports instructions per step. nbody is ~664/step on x86-64 and 1000
steps. Any rv64 figure far from 664,000 says "looping" without disassembling
anything.

THE HOT-PC HISTOGRAM DID NOT COMPLETE, and the approach is the thing to avoid
repeating. Running the whole program under `qemu-riscv64 -one-insn-per-tb -d
exec,nochain` writes one log line per instruction -- 564 million of them -- and
sorting that to find the hottest pc hit the container 1800s timeout (exit 124).

Cheaper ways to the same answer, for whoever picks this up:

  - Do not sort the whole trace. `tail -c` a few MB of the log and histogram
    only that: a spinning loop is by definition what the program is doing at
    the end, so the tail is representative and the head is not needed.
  - Better, skip the trace entirely. The program is non-terminating, so
    ATTACHING is enough -- run it, wait a second, and sample the pc. Any
    sample lands in the loop.
  - Cheapest of all, and the one I keep failing to reach for first: compile at
    a small N and compare instructions retired against the x86-64 figure. The
    harness already does exactly this. nbody is ~664 instructions per step, so
    N=10 should retire a few thousand; a figure orders of magnitude off names
    the problem without any tracing at all.

The 18-latch inventory in the previous note still stands and narrows it: two
latches are the runtime loops and both are proven to terminate, so the spin is
in one of the 16 compiled ones.
close_reason:
MET. nbody compiles to RV64 and runs under qemu-riscv64 producing energies
bit-identical to the x86-64 build and to bench/nbody/SPEC.md -- the same oracle
the x86-64 target is held to, which is the acceptance as written.

The driver takes a target; the encoder has ecall; build-executable emits EM_RISCV;
the runtime provides entry, heap, command line, exit, %make-flvector and all six
externs plus the check traps; and ten defects between selection and the ABI are
fixed (D77, D81). Asserted in rv64-test.ss so it cannot regress silently.

title: qemu-count.sh and callgrind disagree by 6.17% on sonic binaries and 0.0000% on gcc's
description:
Two instruments, same binary, same N, compared by SLOPE between N=200 and
N=400 so process startup cancels and only loop body remains. Neither run
reported an uncounted block, so nothing is being silently dropped:

    ref-scalar (gcc -O2)   callgrind 130781   qemu 130781   +0.0000%
    sonic                  callgrind 132800   qemu 141000   +6.1747%

41 instructions per step, on our own output only. Exact agreement on gcc and
6% on us is not instrument spread -- one of the two is wrong about our
binaries specifically.

WHY IT MATTERS: qaq.10 exists because callgrind cannot run racket, sbcl, ecl
or clisp, and qemu-count.sh was built to answer for them. Any milestone that
compares sonic (callgrind) against sbcl (qemu) is then a cross-instrument
ratio. I had been describing that as agreeing to about 1%, which I had never
measured. It does not.

LEADING SUSPECT, untested: qemu-count.sh counts instructions per block by
decoding the OBJD-T bytes with objdump -D -b binary -m i386:x86-64. That
decodes a raw byte stream with no symbol or boundary information. A block
whose bytes resynchronise differently there than they do in the ELF would be
credited with a wrong instruction count on EVERY execution of that block,
which is exactly the shape of the error -- a fixed per-step offset on a hot
block. gcc emits conventional encodings; we hand-roll ours, so a systematic
decode difference showing up only on our binaries fits.

RULED OUT ALREADY:
  - uncounted blocks: the no-in_asm-record note fired on neither binary
  - startup accounting: the slope cancels it, and ref-scalar is exact
  - retranslation accumulation: the parser accumulated OBJD-T bytes across
    retranslations of one address; fixed, and the totals did not move

THE EXPERIMENT: find the hottest block in the sonic log, then compare its
instruction count as counted by objdump-on-raw-bytes against
objdump -d on the real ELF restricted to that address range. If they differ,
that is the bug and it is in our script. If they agree, the suspect is wrong
and the next place to look is whether callgrind and qemu differ on some
instruction form we emit and gcc does not.
acceptance_criteria:
Either the 6.17% is explained and eliminated, so both instruments agree on
sonic to the same 0.0000% they already reach on ref-scalar; or it is explained
and shown to be a genuine instrument difference, in which case count-slope.sh
must refuse a cross-instrument RATIO the way it already refuses a
cross-instrument slope, and no milestone may be answered by one.
notes:
LEADING SUSPECT RULED OUT, with data.

The description proposed that this script miscounts instructions per block,
because it decodes OBJD-T bytes with objdump -D -b binary, which has no
boundary information. Tested directly.

First attempt was invalid and worth recording so nobody repeats it: comparing
against objdump -d on the ELF returned ZERO instructions for every block.
Our emitted binary has NO SECTION HEADERS -- readelf says "There are no
sections in this file", just two LOAD program headers at 0x400000 and
0x600000 -- and objdump -d disassembles only marked sections. It reports
nothing and exits 0, which reads like an empty block rather than a tool that
could not do the job. Any check of our emitted binaries has to use -D with an
explicit offset, or go at the bytes.

Byte-level comparison, file offset = vaddr - 0x400000 since the first LOAD
sits at file offset 0. Ten hottest blocks, at N=200:

    0x401a56  231 bytes  match      0x402001   66 bytes  match
    0x401ead  219 bytes  match      0x401e9c   12 bytes  match
    0x401f8d  112 bytes  match      0x401e09   35 bytes  match
    0x401ffd    4 bytes  match      0x401a41   16 bytes  match
    0x401b3d    5 bytes  match      0x401c02   11 bytes  match

    blocks whose logged bytes differ from the file: 0

Same objdump, same flags, a stream that starts on a real instruction boundary
and matches the file byte for byte. The block accounting in qemu-count.sh is
sound, and the parser is not the source of the 6.17%.

SO THE DIFFERENCE IS IN WHAT THE TWO TOOLS COUNT. Also ruled out along the
way: uncounted blocks (the no-in_asm-record note fires on neither binary),
startup accounting (the slope cancels it, and ref-scalar agrees exactly), and
retranslation accumulation in the parser (fixed as hygiene; totals unmoved).

NEXT EXPERIMENT, unattempted: callgrind with --dump-instr=yes gives per-
instruction-address counts. Diff those against this script per-block
accounting to localise the 41 instructions per step to an ADDRESS. That turns
the question from "which tool is wrong" into "which instruction do they
disagree about", which is answerable. Arithmetic constraint for whoever picks
it up: 8200 instructions over 200 steps, and no single block explains it --
8200/400 execs = 20.5 and 8200/600 = 13.67, neither an integer, so it is a
combination of blocks or a per-execution effect rather than one bad block.

THE DISAGREEMENT IS N-INDEPENDENT AND EXACT. Re-measured the sonic slope at a
10x larger N pair:

    N= 200..400   callgrind 664.00   qemu 705.00   +6.1747%
    N=2000..4000  callgrind 664.00   qemu 705.00   +6.1747%

Identical to the hundredth at both scales. So this is a genuine per-step
difference of exactly 41 instructions, not a startup or amortisation artifact,
and it will not wash out at any N.

THAT INVALIDATES A CLAIM ON qaq.5, worth flagging because it was load-bearing
there. That bead notes say the two counters "converge to within 0.7% at scale
(ratio 0.9439 at N=200, 0.9965 at N=2000, 1.0071 at N=20000)" and use that to
argue a 3.4x margin is safe across instruments. It cannot have been measured on
this binary as it now stands: if the SLOPES differ by 6.17% and are stable,
then the ratio of TOTALS converges to 1.0617, not to 1.0071. A ratio of totals
approaching 1.0 requires the slopes to agree.

The likeliest reading is that the cross-validation ran on a binary both
instruments agree on -- ref-scalar agrees to +0.0000% -- or predates D59/D64
changing what sonic emits. Either way the 0.7% figure should not be relied on,
and qaq.5 no longer needs it: the comparison there is now single-instrument.

Still unexplained: WHICH 41 instructions. The next experiment stands as
described -- callgrind --dump-instr=yes, diffed per address against this
script per-block accounting.
close_reason:
Root cause found and fixed (D72). It was our own counter, not an instrument
difference. objdump wraps any instruction longer than 7 bytes onto a continuation
line that carries an ADDRESS but no mnemonic, and qemu-count.sh's regex matched
both lines, so every instruction of 8+ bytes was counted twice on every execution
of its block. We emit absolute-addressed forms like 'mov 0x600068,%rbx'; gcc -O2
has none in its hot blocks, which is why it agreed to 0.0000% and we did not.

Found by diffing PER ADDRESS (new harness/count-diff.sh): 954 addresses agreed,
114 were counted by qemu and given zero by callgrind, and none went the other
way -- callgrind's address set being a strict subset is the signature of
over-decoding. After the fix: 954 agree, 3 disagree, +0.0022%, and the slopes
match to the hundredth on both binaries (sonic 664.00/664.00, ref-scalar
653.90/653.90).

Kept: count-diff.sh, because it turns 'these totals differ' into 'they differ at
this address'. Lesson recorded in LOOP.md: validate an instrument on the thing
you intend to measure -- the cross-check had only ever run on gcc's output, where
the bug cannot appear.

title: Five passes in the shipping pipeline have no test file: shapes, elemrange, cse, fold (and dce only incidentally)
description:
E4's acceptance is 'Each pass has fixture tests, and the elision pass removes the bounds check from nbody's inner loop as verified in disassembly.' The second clause is now MET (disasm-test.ss asserts it on the real compiled binary with a control, see qaq.4). The first is not.

MEASURED -- which test files import each pass:

    shapes      0
    elemrange   0
    cse         0
    fold        0
    dce         1  (addrfold-test.ss, incidentally, not as its subject)

All five run in the shipping pipeline: driver.ss calls elemrange (line 44), fold-program (75), cse-program (120), dce-program (131) and shape-facts (322). The tree has 54 test files and these five passes are not the subject of any of them.

shapes.ss is the one that matters most. driver.ss's own comment: 'SHAPES BEFORE ELISION. The interval domain can discharge nbody's inner loop arithmetically and never had the premises: a vector's length was never connected to the make-flvector that produced it, and a top-level (define n-bodies 5) read as unknown. shapes.ss derives both and propagates them across call sites, which is REQUIRED rather than nice -- the kernels take their vectors as PARAMETERS, so a fact that stops at the allocation never reaches the loop that needs it.'

So the pass that supplies the premises for every bounds check we elide -- including the ones Milestone 2 just asserted are gone -- has no direct test. If shapes silently stopped deriving a fact, elision would quietly keep checks and the only signal would be a performance regression nobody attributed to it. Worse in the other direction: if it derived a WRONG fact, elision would remove a check that was needed, which is the unsound-domain failure D24 calls the thing cross-agreement exists to catch.

WORK: a fixture test per pass, in the style of the existing ones -- a hand-written input, the pass, and the expected output, plus at least one case where the pass must REFUSE. For shapes specifically, cover the two premises the comment names: length tied to its make-flvector, and a top-level constant read as known, propagated across a call site.
acceptance_criteria: Each of shapes, elemrange, cse, fold and dce is the subject of a test file with at least one positive case and one refusal.
close_reason: Complete. shapes, elemrange, cse, fold and dce each have a test file, wired into the suite: 9 + 8 + 11 + 10 + 14 = 52 assertions. Two of the five had real defects -- elemrange's escape walk read the extern list instead of the program body (D62, a live soundness bug that could discharge a needed check), and shapes/cse/fold/dce were clean. Three of the five fixtures first passed VACUOUSLY, which is worth recording as the hazard of testing an unfamiliar IR: a fixture the pass declines makes every refusal assertion pass for the wrong reason.

title: callgrind cannot run racket, sbcl, ecl or clisp, so measure.sh cannot compare against them

WHAT IT BLOCKS. Milestone 3 (qaq.5) is worded 'harness/measure.sh AND harness/bench.sh both show SonicScheme ahead of sbcl-5, with a bootstrap CI excluding 1.0'. The bench.sh arm passes decisively -- baseline sbcl-5, ratio 0.1709, 95% CI [0.1552, 0.1843], i.e. 5.85x faster with the interval nowhere near 1.0. The measure.sh arm cannot be produced for sbcl-5 by any means currently available, since the PMU is gone and the simulator refuses.

OPTIONS, none of which are the agent's to pick: accept wall-clock alone for the milestones that name a managed-runtime Lisp; restrict measure.sh's instruction arm to the configs it can measure and say so in its output; or find a third instrument. Note measure.sh remains fully usable for sonic vs C, vs Ada and vs Chez, which is where the instruction-level comparisons in the ledger actually live.
acceptance_criteria: Either measure.sh can count sbcl-5, or the milestones that name it are re-worded to the instrument that exists, with the reasoning recorded.
notes:
CLISP DIAGNOSED: the counter's boundary is now understood, and it is not "clisp is fast".

The program is fine. clisp responds to N correctly and identically native and emulated:

    native  N=50  -0.169075164 -0.169063618      qemu  N=50  -0.169075164 -0.169063618
    native  N=200 -0.169075164 -0.169026909      qemu  N=200 -0.169075164 -0.169026909

So it does different work at different N, under qemu, and gets the right answer.

But the QEMU LOG IS BYTE-IDENTICAL at both: 34,578 lines, 22,542 Trace lines, for N=50 and N=200 alike. And 22,542 block executions is far too few for a bytecode interpreter running nbody at all. qemu's -d logging is therefore not capturing the whole execution -- clisp re-executes itself, and the child's log replaces the parent's, so what is counted is a prologue.

THE COUNTER IS ONLY VALID FOR A PROGRAM QEMU LOGS END TO END. That is not knowable in advance and must be checked per configuration, which is exactly what the two-N protocol does:

    COUNT AT TWO VALUES OF N AND REQUIRE THE NUMBERS TO DIFFER.

An invariant count means the measurement is not measuring the program. It caught c-native (crashes on AVX-512 and yields a partial total) and clisp (exits cleanly, right answer, truncated log). Neither looked wrong on its own, and no other check found either.

REVISED STATUS -- what can be counted on this host, and by what:

    sonic, c-scalar, chez     callgrind. Existing ledger numbers unaffected.
    c-native                  NEITHER. -march=native emits AVX-512; valgrind's
                              VEX cannot decode it and QEMU's TCG does not
                              implement it. This is Milestone 5's reference.
    clisp-9                   NEITHER. Fails the two-N check under qemu.
    sbcl-5, racket-4, ecl-9   qemu produced numbers; NOT two-N validated, and
                              racket and ecl are slow enough under nochain that
                              the check timed out at ten minutes.

So the honest summary is narrower than it looked two iterations ago: qemu extends coverage to some configurations callgrind cannot run, has NOT been shown to cover all four, and cannot help with c-native at all. The wall-clock arm of M3 never depended on any of this and is unaffected (sonic 5.85x ahead of sbcl-5, 95% CI [0.1552, 0.1843]).
sbcl-5 NOW TWO-N VALIDATED, which is the row that matters for M3.

    sbcl-5 N=50   3,174,247
    sbcl-5 N=200  3,509,281      varies with work -> a real measurement

Per-step slope 2233.56 instructions, against sonic's 664.13 from callgrind: sonic retires 3.4x fewer per step. Recorded on qaq.5.

Revised coverage table:

    sonic, c-scalar, chez     callgrind
    sbcl-5                    qemu, two-N VALIDATED
    racket-4, ecl-9           qemu produced numbers, NOT validated (both time
                              out under nochain past ten minutes)
    clisp-9                   NEITHER -- qemu's log is byte-identical at N=50
                              and N=200 because clisp re-execs and the child's
                              log replaces the parent's, so only a prologue is
                              counted
    c-native                  NEITHER -- -march=native emits AVX-512 here;
                              VEX cannot decode it, TCG does not implement it

So the decision is now well-posed. Option (a), "measure.sh can count sbcl-5", is ACHIEVED for the configuration M3 names, at the cost of a second instrument in the same table. It is NOT achievable for c-native, which Milestone 5 names -- that one needs option (b) or (c) regardless.

RESOLVED IN MECHANISM (D68). The open question on this bead had been framed as
a decision for Nathan: may a milestone be answered by two instruments agreeing
to about 1%? That framing was wrong twice over.

FIRST, the 1% was never measured. I wrote it into count-slope.sh header
without checking. Measured, by slope between N=200 and N=400 so startup
cancels:

    ref-scalar (gcc -O2)   callgrind 130781   qemu 130781   +0.0000%
    sonic                  callgrind 132800   qemu 141000   +6.1747%

Exact on gcc output, 6.17% on ours. So the tolerance the decision was about
does not exist. Tracked as qaq.11, which rules out the block-decode suspect
with byte-level evidence.

SECOND, and this is the actual resolution, THE DECISION IS UNNECESSARY. The
problem is only ever a RATIO between two configs counted by different tools.
Force ONE instrument across both sides and it disappears: whichever tool is
right about the absolute number, both sides are counted the same way, so the
ratio is sound. Added SONIC_INSTRUMENT=qemu|callgrind. It REFUSES rather than
falling back when the forced instrument cannot run the program, because a
fallback silently restores the mix the force exists to prevent.

A milestone against sbcl therefore runs BOTH sides under qemu, qemu being the
only instrument that can run sbcl at all. The default -- prefer callgrind,
fall back -- stays right for looking at one config in isolation, where the
ledger existing callgrind figures are the comparable ones.

ALSO FIXED, and it had been masking this bead the whole time: the container
working_dir is /work/sonic, but every caller and this script own usage example
write paths relative to the REPO ROOT, so build/nbody/sonic never resolved and
came back as "no instrument could count this program" -- a missing path
reported as a limitation of the instruments. Resolves against the repo root
now, and a missing file gets a DIFFERENT refusal message from an instrument
declining.

Verified, all four paths:
    relative form (was broken)         664.00 instructions/step  callgrind
    forced qemu, same binary           705.00 instructions/step  qemu
    missing program                    refuses, names the path
    forced callgrind on AVX-512        refuses, says the force removed fallback
