Spill and reload are NOT fsd/fld -- a v register is not 64 bits and the width is vtype-dependent. Whole-register vs1r.v/vl1r.v are the forms that do not depend on the current vtype, which is the point: a spill path that reads CSR state is a spill path that breaks when the state changes.
acceptance_criteria: A packed pair can be allocated to a v register, spilled and reloaded, with a not-inert test (validated by breaking it, per D133/D146). No effect on x86-64 and no effect on scalar RV64 -- nbody still runs bit-identically to x86-64 (D81), which is the agreement any vector work must not break.
notes:
DONE for the allocation half (D170). raw-f64x2 storage class, v1..v31 pool on
arch-rv64 (v0 excluded -- RVV names it as the mask in the encoding), reg-class
'vector, assignment-ok? and pool-for wired, physical? follows from reg-class.
Added as an eighth arch field derived from the target name inside make-arch, the
way mask was, so no constructor call site changed.

Ten checks in regalloc-test.ss including end-to-end allocation of packed vregs
beside raw-word ones. Validated by pointing pool-for at the float pool: fails
with 'a packed pair outside the vector file loses its second lane'.

SPILL IS NOT IMPLEMENTED, it is refused with the three missing pieces named
(vs1r.v/vl1r.v, an address register, a 16-byte slot). That was deliberate -- the
alternative was emitting sd on a v register, which assembles and is wrong. The
refusal's own not-inert validation is deferred to qaq.13.2, which builds the
first program that can reach it.

Suite 8627 / 0 / 63.
close_reason: D170: vector storage class and v-register pool implemented and tested. Spill deliberately refused rather than miscompiled; that work is scoped on this bead's successor.

title: bench.sh and measure.sh run a binary they did not build
description:
D166 fixed the immediate breakage (generated driver scripts carried host paths into the container, so compile.sh sonic always failed on this host) but not the hazard that made it invisible. bench.sh and measure.sh take a configuration name, look up cfg_run_*, and execute whatever binary is at that path. They never compile. So a failed or skipped compile leaves the previous binary in place and both harnesses measure it, reporting a number that looks entirely normal -- which is how an allocator change came back as 696.00 instructions/step both with and without it, off a binary fifty-one minutes stale.

disasm-sonic.sh has the answer in its header: it COMPILES rather than accepting a binary, and there is no way to pass it one, precisely because analysing a stale artifact produces plausible wrong findings. That argument applies verbatim here and these two are the instruments the project's headline numbers come from.
design: Make cfg_compile_* run before cfg_run_* for every configuration named on the command line, unconditionally, and fail the whole run if any compile fails. Rebuilding is seconds against measurement runs of minutes, so there is no reason to make it conditional or to stat mtimes -- a freshness check is one more thing that can be wrong in the direction of silence.
acceptance_criteria: bench.sh and measure.sh compile every configuration they are asked to measure and abort on a compile failure. Demonstrated by breaking a compile deliberately and watching the harness refuse to report a number, which is the D133/D146 convention: an assertion is not finished until you have watched it fail.
close_reason: D168: cfg_build_all compiles every named config before measuring and refuses on failure. Validated by breaking a compile deliberately -- which found the guard inert, because cfg_compile_* swallowed failures on the in-container branch. Fixed in all six.

title: Unroll where it discharges checks, not unconditionally
description:
DECISION FOR NATHAN. One line: keeping unroll-program on by default buys nbody the property "emits NO bounds check at all", which is worth 0.17% of nbody time, and costs 4.7% of fannkuch time.

THE MEASUREMENT, layout-swept per D105 (four pad values per arm, ranges non-overlapping):

  unroll ON   fannkuch mean 9,779.3M cycles     nbody 14 bounds branches -> 0
  unroll OFF  fannkuch mean 9,316.6M cycles     nbody 0 bounds branches -> 14

  nbody cycles move 0.17%, inside its noise, either way.

WHY THE TRADE EXISTS. Unrolling duplicates the loop body, which is what lets the
interval analysis discharge nbody indices (D118). It also doubles the hot loop
branch targets, and 25.2% of fannkuch cycles are front-end stalled on mispredicts
(D112), so the duplication costs more there than the checks it removes.

WHAT IS NOT THE QUESTION. This is not safety versus speed: with unrolling off,
fannkuch has FEWER bounds checks (3, against 6) and is faster. Only nbody loses
the zero-checks property. D116 and D117 framed it as a safety trade and both were
wrong; D118 counted and settled it.

OPTIONS
  (a) keep unrolling: nbody keeps zero checks, fannkuch stays 4.7% slower
  (b) turn it off: fannkuch gains 4.7%, nbody emits 14 bounds branches
  (c) make it conditional on whether it discharges checks -- sound but doubles
      compile time, since elision needs the unrolled form so the count is not
      knowable beforehand
  (d) dissolve it: if the analysis could discharge nbody checks on the ROLLED
      loop there is nothing to trade. Why it cannot is UNEXPLAINED -- see notes;
      three prescriptions for measuring it were written and all three withdrawn.

RECOMMENDATION: (d) is worth one careful attempt before (a) or (b), because it
is the only option that costs nothing. The measurement it needs must distinguish
a site final verdict from its history, and must be validated against a
configuration with a known nonzero answer first.
acceptance_criteria: The pass is applied on the basis of a measured check count rather than unconditionally. fannkuch instruction count and cycles both improve against the unrolled baseline (27,034,305,919 instructions, 9,926.6M mean cycles across four layout-pad values); nbody keeps "emits NO bounds check at all"; both oracles pass; suite green. If the compile-twice cost is judged unacceptable, record that decision here and close -- the measurement stands either way.
notes:
D122: the number is now 4.7%, not 5.6%. D121's merge-identical-functions recovered about 1.3% of it by deduplicating the copies, but the unrolled loop still executes the doubled body -- one function called twice instead of two called once -- so the dynamic branch count is unchanged, and that is what a 25.2% front-end stall is made of. Measured with merging active in both arms, three layout-pad values each: unroll ON mean 9,779.3M cycles, unroll OFF mean 9,316.6M, ranges non-overlapping. The trade is unchanged in shape: nbody's 'emits NO bounds check at all' is worth 0.17% of nbody's time and costs 4.7% of fannkuch's.
D123: the trade may be dissolvable rather than decidable. It exists only because unrolling is what makes elision work (D118). If the analysis could discharge nbody's fourteen checks on the ROLLED loop, unrolling could be switched off and both properties kept -- 4.7% of fannkuch with nbody's elision intact.

Why a duplicated body tells the analysis something the rolled one does not is UNEXPLAINED. Two structural explanations checked and both wrong: the interval domain does handle loops (iv-widen is present), and elide.ss is interprocedural rather than per-function (see its own comments at lines 78 and 468).

HOW TO ANSWER IT: compile nbody with unroll-size-budget 0 and ask elide.ss which sites it failed to prove and what interval it held for the index at each; then the same with unrolling on. The difference is the fact unrolling supplies. That report is one the pass already produces internally.

Do not answer it by inference -- three structural guesses in this session (D94, D101, D123) were refuted by looking.
CORRECTION (D125). BOTH earlier prescriptions on this bead are wrong; do not follow them.

D123 said: measure which sites elide fails to prove, with and without unrolling. D124 said: measure at ABCD instead, because elide is not what discharges the checks. Both wrong. abcd.ss is called FROM elide.ss line 314 as one of the ways elide answers a bounds query -- the 'Stage 07' in its header is a module label, not a pipeline position. There is no later pass.

And D124's evidence for that claim was an instrument error: elide-stats-sites is a mutable accumulator and elide-to-fixpoint runs repeatedly, so a site kept in round one and proved in round three still appears as kept. The diagnostic printed the union across rounds, not the final state.

WHAT STANDS: the mechanism, documented in elide.ss -- a loop variable's range is derived at the call site by sigma refinement on the guard and dies there, because lifting made the loop body a separate procedure whose parameters arrive with no facts; the interval round-trips through the driver as a premise. Unrolling puts two iterations in one procedure and skips the round-trip.

A useful measurement must distinguish a site's FINAL verdict from its history: read the last round's stats, or count chk nodes still marked checked in the program elide-to-fixpoint returns.
D126: all three prescriptions withdrawn (D123 measure at elide, D124 measure at ABCD, D125 count chk nodes in p1). The third attempt produced a third instrument error -- walking a nanopass record as an s-expression, then reporting zero for both checked AND unchecked after unparsing, which means the traversal finds no chk nodes at all.

ESTABLISHED: unrolling is what makes nbody's elision work (14 bounds branches in the finished BINARY without it, 0 with -- D118, measured on the binary, not on a pass's self-report). The mechanism is documented in elide.ss: a loop variable's range is derived at the call site and dies there because lifting made the loop body a separate procedure whose parameters arrive with no facts. The trade is real as measured: nbody's zero checks cost 4.7% of fannkuch (D122).

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the premise round-trip is what fails on the rolled loop, and so whether supplying that fact directly would dissolve the trade.

BEFORE MEASURING: validate the instrument against a configuration with a KNOWN nonzero answer. Three attempts reported zeros that were the instrument rather than the program.
D148: THE MEASUREMENT WORKS NOW. D126's three instrument errors were all the same mistake -- there are no chk nodes in Lssa. A check is a control on a primcall: (primcall make-flvector ((type-check checked)) ...), which is D5's representation and is in lang.ss's grammar.

Corrected, and validated by producing nonzero differentiated counts:

  unroll ON   382 bounds checks before elide -> 161 after  (58% discharged)
  unroll OFF  175 before -> 91 after                       (48% discharged)

Unrolling roughly doubles the sites and improves the discharge rate by ten points.

WHAT REMAINS, now localised rather than open: the finished binary has ZERO bounds branches with unrolling on and fourteen without (D118, counted on emitted code), but elide leaves 161 and 91. Some stage AFTER elide discharges 161 in one configuration and 77 of 91 in the other. Identify it -- the same technique works, add a stage marker after each candidate and count with the corrected walk. The probe is in D148's commit message and takes about ten lines.
D149: cse, addrfold and dce discharge NO bounds checks -- the count leaving elide (161 with unrolling, 91 without) is the count reaching selection.

So the drop to the binary's 0 and 14 (D118) happens at or after selection, OR the binary counter is narrower than 'a check exists'. The second is now more likely: 161 checks becoming zero branches is a large claim for a lowering step, and that counter has never been validated against a known-nonzero configuration.

NEXT STEP, and do this before any further counting: compile nbody with checks forced ON (policy) and confirm the branch-to-sonic-bounds-error count is large. If it is not, D118's zero-and-fourteen is itself the error and several entries rest on it.

Four instrument errors have occurred in this investigation -- an accumulator misread, a record-versus-list walk, the wrong node type, and possibly this counter. Each was found by the next attempt, none by review.
D150: the two counters contradict, and the next step is one line.

Selection lowers every 'chk bounds-check checked' to 'cmp' plus 'jge (label sonic-bounds-error)' -- target-x86-64.ss, unambiguous. So these must agree and do not:

  Lmach, still checked          161 (unroll on)   91 (off)
  finalized, jge to the label     0               14

Both counters were inspected, not assumed: the Lmach shape was printed and the filter matches it; D118's counter matches the emitted form and reports nonzero on fannkuch (3 and 6).

LEADING CANDIDATE: the 161 are in code that never reaches the image. partition-into-functions drops blocks no entry reaches -- the suite asserts 'a procedure nothing calls is dropped, with its inner loop'. Checks inside a dropped function are counted at Lmach and emitted nowhere, which would make both counters correct and the comparison meaningless.

NEXT STEP, one line: count Lmach checks AFTER partition-into-functions rather than before, and see whether 161 becomes 0 and 91 becomes 14. If so the contradiction dissolves and D118 stands unqualified.

The comparison that matters remains D118's, on emitted code: fourteen versus zero.
D151 RESOLVES IT. Counting after partition-into-functions and reachable-functions:

                 at lmach   reachable only
  unroll ON         161           0
  unroll OFF         91          14

The reachable column is D118's emitted-code count exactly. The 161 and 91 were in blocks no entry reaches. Both counters were right and counting different programs.

D118 stands unqualified: unrolling is what discharges nbody's bounds checks, fourteen against zero, on code that ships.

A lmach/reachable marker now exists so a check count can be taken against the program that reaches the image.

OPTION (d)'s NEXT STEP is now about the compiler rather than the measurement: the fourteen checks surviving on the rolled loop are nameable -- print them rather than count them, via the same marker. nbody's indices are all 3i+k against a length proved at allocation, so if the fourteen share that shape, whether elide can reach them without the duplicated induction step is a specific question about elide.ss.
D152: THE TRADE IS SMALLER THAN STATED, AGAIN. The fourteen bounds checks that survive with unrolling off are: subtract-pairs 4, loop%12.57 4, energy-from 6. NONE is in inner%24, the pairwise force loop.

The source shows what those are: offset-momentum! runs once before the loop, energy runs twice (before and after), and advance! runs N times -- five million at the measured configuration. So the checks unrolling discharges are in setup and teardown, and the hot loop emits none either way. That is why nbody's cycles do not move: there was never hot code to slow down.

SO THE DECISION IS: fourteen bounds checks in code that runs O(1) times, against 4.7% of fannkuch's total runtime. The nbody side is not a performance cost at all -- it is the claim 'nbody emits NO bounds check at all', a statement about what the compiler can prove, worth whatever that is worth on D5 and D24's grounds rather than on speed.

Fourth reframing of this decision: D116 called it safety against speed, D117 corrected the direction, D118 counted, D152 locates the counts. Each made the question smaller.
close_reason:
DISSOLVED, not decided. Option (d) was right: the analysis can discharge nbody's checks on the ROLLED loop, and it needed one constant. elide-to-fixpoint carries (define ascent-rounds 4); at 12 the rolled loop discharges all fourteen, same as unrolling. The comment beside the constant explains why 4 looked sufficient -- 'i < n-bodies gives [0,5] in three rounds' -- which is true of the parameter it names and not of the fourteen in subtract-pairs, loop%12.57 and energy-from.

Shipped: ascent-rounds 4->12, unroll-size-budget defaults to 0, unroll-test.ss parameterises its budget so its assertions are not vacuous.

Result, four layout-pad values per arm: fannkuch 9,779.3M -> 9,318.5M cycles, -4.71%, ranges non-overlapping; nbody +0.2% cycles (inside noise) and +6.9% instructions (free per D89); both benchmarks still emit ZERO bounds checks. Suite 8613/61, smoke and containment green.

unroll-program is kept, not deleted: correct, and a target whose front end is not the bottleneck would want it. See D153.

title: A free register goes unused while a value spills in count-flips
description:
D102: the raw pool is (rcx rdx rsi rdi r10 r11 r13 r14). count-flips writes r13 r14 rax rbx rcx rdx and never touches r11. r11 is allocatable rather than scratch, is written by NEITHER of the two callees (both write r10 rax rbx rcx rdi rdx rsi), is not the argument register either call site fills (one raw argument each, so rcx), and is not a return register (rax rcx rdx). It is free across the whole function -- and the incremented flip counter spills to the stack and is incremented there with a read-modify-write per iteration, in a block that is 18.22% of the sampled profile.

Three explanations, none established: (a) the interval-to-destroyed-registers map that regalloc.ss calls "across" contains r11 for a reason not visible in the listing; (b) linear scan ordering never offers it; (c) the spill decision is taken before the register is known free. Distinguish these before changing anything.
acceptance_criteria: Which of the three holds is established by evidence. If the register is genuinely available, count-flips.loop keeps its counter in a register with no rsp read-modify-write, and fannkuch's deterministic instruction count falls against 27,033,942,394 with both oracles passing. If it is unavailable for a real reason, that reason is recorded here and in regalloc.ss and this closes.
close_reason: Answered by D103, and none of the three explanations was right. Instrumenting both spill paths: 21 spills in fannkuch, ALL reporting bad=ALL with a FULL pool. The pool was never the constraint. across answers with the whole register file for a runtime routine, and a second probe named them -- next->display (20), next->newline (16), main.entry1->%make-vector (6). Those routines write 4, 1 and 3 registers respectively and are charged with twelve. Fix filed as qaq.28.

title: Fold a constant into a plain copy; 21 sites in 31% of fannkuch's profile
description: D99: peephole.ss folds constants into arithmetic consumers only -- foldable-use? requires imul or (add sub and or cmp). A plain copy has the same shape, and fannkuch materialises a constant then copies it 21 times, in blocks that are ~31% of the sampled profile ('mov rdi,1' then 'mov rcx,rdi' where 'mov rcx,1' is the whole instruction). Adding 'mov' with a REGISTER destination to foldable-use? is a two-line change and is NOT sufficient: on a base with D99's barrier fix it still fails fannkuch's SPEC.md oracle. TWO hypotheses were checked and refuted, so do not re-derive them: (1) redefines? is a whitelist that misses add/sub/imul writing a register -- searched, ZERO such sites in fannkuch; (2) folding across a basic-block join -- peephole-runs already flushes at every label. Note also the fold trades a 3-byte copy for a 7-byte immediate move, so it is only a win where the materialisation then dies.
acceptance_criteria: The mechanism behind the fannkuch oracle failure is identified by evidence, not inference, and stated. Either the rule lands with the eleven-way bit-exact oracle and the SPEC.md oracle both passing and fannkuch's deterministic instruction count falling against 27,034,212,993, or the rule is shown unsound in general and this bead closes with that argument recorded.
close_reason: Mechanism found by bisection and fixed; optimisation declined on measurement. Partitioning the fold by destination register: each alone passed, all thirteen failed, minimal pair (rdi r13). Cause: fold 1 puts a constant in r13, 'sub %rdx,%r13' modifies it, and redefines? lists only mov/movsd/movzx/lea/cvtsi2sd so the run continued past a write. D99's search for this shape found zero because it searched the INPUT -- the shape exists only in code the pass produces after its own rewrite. Fixed with modifies?, which stops the run at any write to r in both the scan and fold-run, kept separate from redefines? because two-address arithmetic reads its destination and must not license deleting the materialisation. The copy fold itself measures at -0.001% on fannkuch and +0.0003% on nbody -- the materialisation survives, so the copy is replaced rather than removed while code size grows 7 bytes for 3. Reverted with the measurement recorded in peephole.ss. See D100.

title: The clobber analysis answers 'assume everything' for calls into loops
description: D94: threading destroys-of through the precolored path was necessary but not sufficient -- fannkuch's emitted code is byte-identical after it, and count-flips.loop still spills its counter (mov %r13,0x8(%rsp); addq $0x1,0x8(%rsp)) across a call to loop%2.14@8.373, which is a LEAF writing only r10/rax/rbx/rcx/rdi/rdx/rsi and never r13. Something upstream returns #f for that callee. regalloc.ss names three cases that get #f: unknown callee, runtime routine, member of a recursive cycle. In this compiler a loop is a letrec-bound procedure that tail-calls itself (unroll.ss header), so if the cycle test runs over the IR call graph rather than the emitted control flow -- where a self-tail-call is a jmp, not a call -- then every loop is a recursive cycle and every call into one is unanalysable. Determine which case fires and whether the cycle test can use the emitted control flow.
acceptance_criteria: The case returning #f for loop%2.14@8.373 is identified by evidence, not inference. If it is the cycle rule and self-tail-calls can be excluded soundly, count-flips.loop keeps its counter in a register (no rsp read-modify-write in the hot loop) and fannkuch's INSTRUCTION count -- deterministic per D94 -- falls against 27,847,0xx,xxx; the SPEC.md oracle still passes; suite stays green.
close_reason: Premise refuted by D95. The call graph built from the emitted listing is a DAG with no cycles -- a self-tail-call is emitted as jmp and never appears as a call edge, so callee-first never reaches its cycle fallback and the clobber analysis had the callee's real write set all along. The spill is register pressure instead: both callees write 5 of the 8 raw-pool registers, leaving only r11/r13/r14 alive across a call, and count-flips has more than three live values. See qaq.23.

title: Live-range-scoped precoloring: pinned parameters cost their register for the whole function
description: D93: fannkuch's listing is 1103 instructions of which 130 (11.8%) are register-to-register moves, against 20 stack reloads, 11 spills and 3 check-trap references. Checks are elided and spill traffic is modest, so copies are the largest block of instructions doing no arithmetic. This matters on fannkuch specifically and NOT on nbody: D89 measured nbody's surplus instructions as free (removing 465M made it slower), but fannkuch runs 2.48x the instructions for 1.167x the cycles, and at our own IPC of 2.80 gcc's instruction count would take 3.97B cycles against its actual 8.46B. The specializer is not the tool -- at budget 4 and 8 it adds instructions and cycles, since fannkuch's trip counts are data-dependent and no guard folds.
acceptance_criteria: Register-to-register moves in the fannkuch listing fall materially below 130; instructions measured by harness/vm-perf.sh fall against D93's 27,632,610,299 baseline AND cycles fall against 9,871,805,287 -- both, since D89 showed instruction count alone is not a proxy for time; fannkuch's answer still matches the SPEC.md oracle; suite stays green.
notes:
D107 scoping. 110 of the moves are in compiled code (26 are hand-written runtime the allocator never sees), 86 have a source dying at the move, and they concentrate in the hot blocks -- 7 of count-flips.loop's 24 instructions, 6 each in loop%2.372.loop and loop%2.14.434.loop, blocks that are 39% of the profile.

The shape is argument setup: 'mov r14,rdx' then 'mov rcx,r14' then the call, two copies for one value because nothing asked the allocator for rcx.

THE HINT FIX DOES NOT WORK, and this was measured rather than assumed. Adding the reverse direction to move-hints (a vreg moved into a physical register wants that register) is a dozen lines, passes the suite, and changes nothing: listing 1092->1092, moves 136->136, spills 10->10. A counter shows zero physical hints are ever recorded -- an Lmach call carries arguments as OPERANDS and finalize.ss materialises the copies AFTER allocation, so the allocator never sees a physical destination.

The fix is a PRE-COLOURING, not a heuristic: pin a call's operands to the registers that call will require, exactly as parameter-pins already does for incoming parameters, and honour them through allocate-program/precolored. That is an allocation-interface change interacting with everything pins already constrain.
D108: the pin mechanism cannot be reused. parameter-pins returns '() unless every-call-is-tail?, because a non-tail call destroys the argument registers -- which applies doubly to outgoing arguments. And allocate-program/precolored removes each pinned register from the pool for the WHOLE function (callconv.ss:452-458, 528-534): pinning the six raw argument registers would leave two of eight allocatable everywhere, to save two copies per call site.

The fix is RANGE-BASED pre-colouring -- a value constrained to a register over part of its live range and free elsewhere. Linear scan here has no such notion; a pin is a property of the function, not of an interval. Adding one touches the expiry and eviction logic D95 and D103 were both about. Not a heuristic, not a pin, not small. Kept at P1 for the prize (7 of count-flips.loop's 24 instructions, blocks that are 39% of the profile).
D120 VALUE-CASE AUDIT. This bead's payoff is measured in INSTRUCTIONS, and instruction count is measured NOT to convert to time on either benchmark: nbody's spare instructions are free (D89 -- 465M removed, 18M cycles slower), and on fannkuch removing 863M instructions and 861M branches cost 3.5% wall clock (D111) because 25.2% of its cycles are front-end stalled on mispredicts (D112). Nothing here is wrong and the work may still be worth doing for code quality, but it should not be scheduled expecting a speedup. The two beads that target a measured bottleneck are qaq.29 (merging the duplicated reversal functions removes branch TARGETS, which is what the front end is stalling on) and qaq.30 (same mechanism, already measured at 5.6%).
D143 staleness check: the count is now 118, not 130. merge-identical-functions (D121, D130, D132) removed duplicate functions and their copies of these moves. The analysis in D107 stands -- they are argument setup, the allocator never sees the physical destination, and the fix is a range-based pre-colouring the linear scan has no notion of (D108) -- but any future measurement should be taken against 118.

D163 REPRIORITISES THIS TO P2. Mapped cycle profile at n=11, against the
instruction mix of the listing that built the profiled binary:

  function                  prof%  insns  r2r mov  spill
  loop%2.224.loop           34.58     19        5      0
  loop%2.14@8.225.loop      17.16     18        3      0
  count-flips.loop          15.61     19        6      0
  copy-perm.loop            10.12     16        3      0
  next.loop                  9.36     54       12     12

The top four blocks are 77.5% of the profile and 17 of their 72 instructions are
register-to-register copies -- 23.6% of the hot-path work moves a value between
registers, and count-flips is a third copies. Upper bound if every copy vanished
and cycles followed instructions there: ~18% of total cycles. Real figure will be
lower; it is still an order above anything else open.

D120's blanket 'instructions do not convert to time on fannkuch' DOES NOT APPLY
HERE. It rests on D111, which removed 863M instructions AND 861M BRANCHES and got
3.5% slower, explained by D112's 25.2% front-end stall on mispredicts. A register
copy is not a branch; removing it removes decode and fetch pressure, which is the
resource D112 named as constrained. The two experiments push on opposite things.

D165 REDIRECTS THIS BEAD. The copies are a SYMPTOM and the pass this bead names
(coalescing) already exists in regalloc.ss as move-hints, works, and cannot help.

fannkuch's hottest block, loop%2.224.loop, 34.58% of the profile, 19 instructions:
  4015ad  mov %rcx,%rsi      <- copy in
  4015b0  mov %rdx,%rdi      <- copy in
          ... body works entirely in rsi/rdi/r10/r11 ...
  4015dd  lea 0x1(%rsi),%r10
  4015e1  lea -0x1(%rdi),%rsi
  4015e5  mov %r10,%rcx      <- copy back
  4015e8  mov %rsi,%rdx      <- copy back
  4015eb  jmp 0x4015ad
Four of five copies are the loop's phi shuffle across the back edge.

CAUSE: x86-64 raw-word args are (rcx rdx rsi rdi r10 r11), so a 2-parameter
function pins param 0 to rcx and param 1 to rdx. allocate-program/precolored*
implements a pin by REMOVING the register from every pool and hiding the vreg
from the scan -- the pin costs that register for the WHOLE FUNCTION, not for the
pinned value's live range. callconv.ss says so in a comment and judges it nearly
free, correctly, for the case it was written for (return placement, end of block,
usually a scratch register). It is not free for a hot loop's parameters.

No hint can fix it: the register the body wants is not in the pool to be
preferred.

THE WORK: make precoloring live-range-scoped inside allocate/scan* -- hold rcx
for the parameter's interval and release it after, so a body vreg starting where
the parameter ends can take it. That is the same register TRANSFER move-hints
already performs for a dying move source (regalloc.ss ~line 708, with the
soundness argument written out). Not another pass over the listing.

DONE (D167). allocate-program/precolored* no longer reduces the pools or hides
the pinned vregs; it hands the scan a table of decided assignments (scan-pins)
and a pinned interval releases its register on expiry like any other.

Deterministic, fresh builds either side:
  nbody     696.00 -> 676.00 instructions/step   -2.87%
  fannkuch  29,877,604,024 -> 26,912,083,639     -9.92%
  listing   573 -> 553 insns, 104 -> 97 copies
fannkuch's hottest block loses both copies IN; the back-edge parallel copy stays.

Suite 8617/0/63 (a new not-inert test, validated by reverting the change and
watching it fail). Both fannkuch oracles agree. RISC-V gate bit-exact at 17 sig
digits.

WALL CLOCK SHOWS NOTHING. fannkuch 3222.9 -> 3258.8 ms min of 9, inside D105's
4.97% alignment band. nbody ratio 1.1036 vs c-native, CI [0.9884, 1.1646],
spanning 1.0. D163's prediction that removing copies would relieve D112's
front-end stall is FALSIFIED. Kept for the structure, not the clock.
close_reason: D167: live-range-scoped precoloring implemented and measured. nbody -2.87% and fannkuch -9.92% instructions, suite green with a not-inert test. No wall-clock effect, recorded honestly.

title: Unrolling does not fire on nbody's pair loop even with a literal bound
description: D88 refuted the D87 hypothesis. unroll-program and unroll-fully both run in the driver, the loop bound is now a literal 5 after gconst, and the branch count is unchanged to five significant figures (300.31M vs C's 65.4M). unroll.ss's header states it needs NO trip count -- it replaces the self tail call with a copy of the body and the copied body carries its own exit test -- which makes the non-firing more surprising, not less. Determine whether the pass declines this loop, fires and is undone downstream, or never identifies it as a loop at all. gcc fully flattens the same ten-iteration loop; that is the 4.6x branch gap.
acceptance_criteria: A stated, evidenced reason why the pair loop is not unrolled -- pass declines it / fires and is reverted / not recognised -- with the deciding condition named in unroll.ss or specialize.ss. If it is a fixable gate, branches measured by harness/vm-perf.sh fall materially below 300.31M with the bit-exact oracle still passing.
close_reason: Answered by D89. Unrolling DOES fire (unroll-program/report: 10 loops on nbody, inner%24 included). The premise was wrong, not the pass. gcc's advantage is deleting the loop, which needs the guard to fold; with gconst it does, and the specializer sweep saturates at budget 8 removing 14% of instructions and 40% of branches -- for MORE cycles. Unrolling further is ruled out by measurement.

title: Cut the 235M excess branches in the nbody hot loop
description: D85 measured sonic-fma at 300.3M branches against ref-native's 65.4M on nbody N=5e6 -- 4.6x, mispredicted at only 0.02%, so they are cheap and perfectly predicted and still occupy issue slots. With IPC already at 3.36 (near issue width) instruction count is what is left, and branches are the largest identified block of it. Expected shape: redundant bounds checks and type checks that dominate a known-safe indexing pattern. fannkuch independently shows the same instruction-count story (2.51x instructions for 1.24x time).
acceptance_criteria: Branch count on nbody N=5e6 measured by harness/vm-perf.sh drops materially against the 300.3M baseline, with instructions falling alongside it; the eleven-way bit-exact cross-agreement oracle still passes; no check is removed that cannot be shown redundant; suite stays green.
notes: D87 root cause: top-level defines are reloaded from memory (43 load sites, 3 in the inner loop body), so n-bodies is a register compare instead of cmp $5 and NO trip count is known -- nothing can unroll. Branch count identical between sonic and sonic-fma (300.30M/300.29M) confirms control flow is untouched by arithmetic fusion. sonic-u4 measured definitively WORSE by counters (962.6M cycles, 3421.8M instr, 320.3M branches): growing the specializer budget without a known bound duplicates work instead of removing control flow.
close_reason: Superseded by D89. The goal was wrong: we removed 120M of the 235M excess branches via the specializer and cycles got WORSE (948.3M -> 966.4M). At 0.02% mispredict those branches were already free. Cutting branches is not the lever; see D89 and qaq.20 for the remaining question.

title: RV64 runtime does not walk argv, so the target cannot be measured per step
description:
qemu-count.sh counts RV64 now, but harness/count-slope.sh REFUSES a slope for
it and is right to:

    N=200 -> 1388713
    N=400 -> 1388713

Identical, because the RV64 entry sequence does not build the command-line
list. `command-line` returns nil, `length` returns 0, `(fx> 0 1)` is false, and
nbody takes its default of N=1000 regardless of the argument passed. The count
is a real count of a real run -- it is just always the same run.

That is precisely the failure the two-N protocol exists to catch (D63): a real
count varies with N, and one that does not means the measurement is not
measuring the program.

CONSEQUENCE: RV64 has no per-step instruction figure, so it cannot be compared
against x86-64 on the instrument this project trusts most, and qaq.13s "not
slower" clause cannot be answered by instruction count either.

WHAT IT NEEDS. The x86-64 entry sequence walks argv backward from argc-1,
calling %cstr->string on each pointer and %cons to build the list. Neither
helper exists on RV64. So this is two runtime routines plus the walk:

  %cstr->string   allocate a string object and copy bytes until NUL
  %cons           allocate a pair

Both are bump-pointer allocations of the shape %make-flvector already has on
RV64, so the pattern is established rather than new.

NOTE the runtime header already records why this was deferred: an empty
command-line takes nbody s default branch, N=1000, "which is the case the
oracle publishes values for". That was the right call while the target could
not run at all. It stops being the right call now that the target works and
cannot be measured.
acceptance_criteria:
harness/count-slope.sh reports an instructions-per-step figure for the RV64
nbody build -- meaning the counts at two different N genuinely differ -- and
build/nbody-rv64 responds to its argument the way the x86-64 build does.
close_reason:
Done. The RV64 runtime walks argv: %rv-cons and %rv-cstr->string build the
command-line list, and cadr and string->number are implemented rather than
trapping. count-slope.sh now reports 1386.00 instructions/step for RV64 against
664.00 for x86-64, and the two targets are bit-identical at N=200, 400 and 1000.

Needed lbu and sb in the encoder (byte-verified against binutils, 77 instructions
total). One bug of my own on the way: string->number read its length at the CDR
offset, which parses a different number without faulting -- caught by comparing
explicit N=1000 against the default, which is also 1000.

title: Milestone 4 on RV64: no packed lowering exists for the target
description:
Split out of qaq.6 on 2026-08-18. M4 originally said "verified in disassembly
on both targets"; the x86-64 half is met and closed, this is the half that is
not.

TWO INDEPENDENT GAPS.

  1. slp.ss packed operations have NO rv64 lowering. p2add, p2sub, p2mul,
     p2splat and p2hi are x86-64:1 and rv64:0 -- their only selection rules
     live in target-x86-64.ss. slp-program is now gated off for rv64 in
     driver.ss for exactly this reason, so an RV64 build is correct scalar
     code with no packed arithmetic to find.

  2. The RV64 target does not yet run nbody at all (1mp.6). It compiles end to
     end and executes 564M instructions before a non-terminating loop takes
     it off the end of an array.

So this needs (2) finished, then (1) written: either the p2* pairs lowered onto
RVV, or the vectorize.ss route wired in -- and note D73 found that route aimed
at the wrong gap for the four-lane question, which does not bear on two-lane
pairs.

WHY IT IS A SEPARATE BEAD rather than a note on qaq.6: the x86-64 claim is
verified today on the real compiled binary and deserves to be closed as such.
Leaving one bead open on a half that needs a whole subsystem would misreport
both halves.
acceptance_criteria:
Packed arithmetic appears in the SONIC-COMPILED nbody inner loop for rv64,
reached through compiled-loop-of on the real binary, AND the packed build is
measured NOT SLOWER than the scalar one on real hardware.

THE SECOND CLAUSE IS THE DECISION (2026-08-18), and it is deliberately harder
than the criterion it replaces. RV64 has no 128-bit SIMD: packed f64 work goes
through RVV, which is length-agnostic and STATEFUL -- `vsetvli` opens a region
that must be re-executed if control rewinds into it, per vec-rv64.ss.

A lowering that emits `vsetvli` before every packed operation would satisfy
"packed arithmetic appears in the disassembly" and would almost certainly be
SLOWER than the scalar code it replaced. That is the measurable-proxy trap this
project refused for M5 (D78): a number that can be quoted, about something other
than the thing being claimed. So the criterion now requires the capability to
pay for itself.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY NEEDS, sized:
  - a VECTOR REGISTER CLASS in regs.ss. There is none today; the allocator
    models value/raw/float only, so v0-v31 cannot be assigned.
  - vsetvli REGION MANAGEMENT, so the state is established once per region
    rather than per operation. vec-rv64.ss already carries this knowledge and
    17 green assertions for it -- and emits LISTINGS rather than vregs, which
    is the wrong output form (D67), so it informs the work without being it.
  - selection rules mapping slp.ss packed ops onto RVV. The ENCODER is ready:
    vsetvli, vfadd.vv, vfsub.vv, vfmul.vv, vfdiv.vv, vfmacc.vv, vle64.v,
    vse64.v and vfmv.v are all present and byte-verified.

NOT ON THE PERFORMANCE PATH, which is why it is P2 rather than P1. D79 measured
that packing was never the gap to gcc -O3 -- we already emit more packed
arithmetic on x86-64 than c-native does -- and D82 gave RV64 the capability that
WAS the gap. So this is milestone completeness and a genuine RVV capability, not
a speed fix.

NOTE ON MEASURING IT: wall clock on RV64 cannot be taken under qemu, which is an
emulator. "Not slower" needs real hardware, or an instruction-count comparison
stated as such.
notes:
UNBLOCKED. This bead was gated on RV64 not running nbody at all; it does now, and
bit-identically to x86-64 (D81). The remaining work is entirely the RVV lowering
described in the acceptance.

Also note what changed underneath it: slp.ss is currently GATED OFF for rv64 in
driver.ss, because its packed ops have no rv64 lowering and an ungated run died
in selection with "target cannot select these ops (p2splat p2mul p2add p2sub
p2hi)". That gate is the right default and is where this work starts -- it should
become a capability test rather than a target-name test once RVV lowering exists.

A CONCRETE REASON BEYOND MILESTONE COMPLETENESS, now that RV64 is measurable
(D83). Contraction measured on both targets:

                instructions/step    with fp-contract
    rv64             1386.00              1291.00      -6.9%
    x86-64            664.00               596.00     -10.2%

x86-64 gains more, and the asymmetry is exactly this bead. On x86-64 a fused
multiply-add replaces two PACKED operations, each doing two lanes; on RV64 it
replaces two scalar ones, because slp is gated off for want of the lowering this
bead is about. So packing and contraction COMPOUND on one target and not the
other -- the RV64 packed lowering is worth more than its own direct saving,
because it also doubles what every subsequent fused multiply-add is worth.

The acceptance clause "not slower" is also answerable now without real hardware:
instructions per step is available for RV64 and stated as such, which is the
alternative that clause already allows.

SIZED PROPERLY, and the register class is the CHEAP half. regalloc dispatches
through one three-case function:

    (define (pool-for arch sc)
      (case sc ((tagged) (arch-value arch))
               ((raw-word) (arch-raw arch))
               ((raw-f64) (arch-float arch))))

and reg-class is a similar cond. The arch record already carries a `mask` field
for AVX-512 k registers, so a `vector` pool is precedented rather than novel.
Adding a class is perhaps an hour across regs.ss, regalloc.ss and callconv.ss.

THE EXPENSIVE HALF IS AN ARCHITECTURAL TENSION IN slp.ss, and it is worth
stating before anyone starts. slp s entire design is that a packed value is an
ORDINARY raw-f64 vreg -- its header: "the register allocator, the static
partition and the collector need no changes at all, because a pair lives exactly
where a scalar double lives". That is true on x86-64, where one xmm holds both
lanes.

It is false on RV64. f registers are 64 bits; a 2-lane f64 pack needs a v
register, which is a different file. So on RV64 a packed value CANNOT be a
raw-f64 vreg, and slp would have to emit a target-dependent storage class --
which is precisely the property its design exists to avoid.

SO THIS IS NOT "EXTEND slp". It is a separate RVV vectorization path, which is
what vectorize.ss and vec-rv64.ss were written for -- they carry the RVV
knowledge, including vsetvli region semantics and 17 green assertions, and emit
LISTINGS rather than vregs, which is the wrong output form (D67). The work is to
produce vregs of a vector class from that knowledge.

Plus vsetvli itself is stateful: a region must be re-entered at its vsetvli if
control rewinds into it, so it is not an instruction that can be emitted
per-operation without cost, and not one a peephole can safely move.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH DOING, from D83: contraction gains 10.2% on x86-64 and
6.9% on RV64, and the difference is exactly this bead -- on x86 a fused
multiply-add folds two PACKED operations, on RV64 two scalar ones. Packing does
not merely add its own saving, it doubles what every subsequent fused
multiply-add is worth.
STALE HALF, CORRECTED (D142). This bead lists two gaps and the SECOND IS CLOSED. It says 'The RV64 target does not yet run nbody at all (1mp.6). It compiles end to end and executes 564M instructions before a non-terminating loop takes it off the end of an array.' That was fixed by D81 and is asserted in the suite today:

  ok  an RV64 image we emit is loaded and run by the kernel, and exits 42
  ok  nbody RUNS on rv64 under qemu
  ok  and its energies are BIT-IDENTICAL to the x86-64 build's

So the sequencing the bead prescribes -- finish (2), then write (1) -- is done in its first half, and the remaining work is only gap (1): slp.ss's p2add, p2sub, p2mul, p2splat and p2hi have no rv64 selection rules, and driver.ss gates slp-program off for rv64 accordingly (line 186, whose own comment says this becomes a capability question when RV64 grows RVV or pairs).

That gap needs the vector subsystem -- a vector register class and stateful vsetvli -- since RV64 without RVV has no packed float at all. It is not reachable in increments that produce a measurable result before the whole path exists, which is why it is the last unstarted item rather than the next one.

D169 DECOMPOSES THIS. The bead reads as five missing selection rules; on x86-64
those rules ARE a table because xmm already is the packed file and the width
rides on the mnemonic. On RV64 none of that holds -- no register class reaches
v0..v31, width is vtype/vl CSR state rather than an opcode, and the convention
says nothing about v registers across a call. Children: qaq.13.1 (storage class
and pool), qaq.13.2 (vsetvli placement), qaq.13.3 (convention). The encoder is
NOT the gap: vec-rv64.ss already does RVV encoding, planning and kernel emission.
close_reason:
M4 on RV64 is not reachable with slp as written; see qaq.13.4.

Everything below the pass is built, tested and inert: storage class and
v-register pool (D170), convention (D171), three encodings byte-verified against
binutils (D172), all nine selection rules (D174, D176), target-aware class-to-file
mapping (D175), and the V permission itself (D182), off by default. The blocker is
not lowering -- it is that slp's cost model is x86-64's, because a scalar reading
lane 0 of a pack is free on xmm and costs a vfmv.f.s on RVV (D183).

Reopen with a decision to give slp a per-target cost model or to write RV64 a
different vectoriser. The x86-64 half of M4 was verified and closed separately.

title: contract.ss has no test: the fp-contract PERMISSION is covered, the pass that obeys it is not
description:
Last pass in the tree that no test file imports, found by sweeping every src pass against every test after cqs.19 closed.

policy-test.ss covers D24's policy half thoroughly -- 'fp-contract is off by default, per D24', and the reasoning that the RISC-V smoke gate found it because RV64 gcc contracts to fmadd.d by default while baseline x86-64 has no FMA to contract into. disasm-test.ss can read contraction back out of a disassembly via contraction-insns.

What is untested is contract.ss itself: the pass that turns a multiply and an add into one fused instruction when the permission is granted. So the PERMISSION is asserted off by default and the PASS that must obey it is not asserted to obey it. If it fused with the permission off, or declined with it on, policy-test.ss would not notice -- it tests the policy resolver, not the transform.

That matters more than an ordinary coverage gap because of what D24 says contraction IS: two roundings becoming one, which changes results. Oracle check 2 is eleven-way BIT-EXACT cross-agreement, and D24 keeps contraction default-off precisely so that check stays meaningful. A pass that fused when it should not would break bit-exactness against the other ten implementations -- which the suite WOULD catch, loudly, via differential-test.ss. The dangerous direction is the quiet one: silently declining to fuse when granted costs the measured 15 cycles D24 records and looks like nothing at all.

WORK: a fixture test in the style of the five from cqs.19. At minimum -- a multiply feeding an add fuses when fp-contract is granted; the identical shape does NOT fuse when it is not; a multiply whose result has another reader does not fuse (fusing would change that reader's value); and reassociation is still refused, which D24 forbids outright.
acceptance_criteria: contract.ss is the subject of a test file asserting it fuses under the permission, declines without it, and declines where a second reader would observe the unfused product.
close_reason: Done. 15 assertions in test/contract-test.ss covering both directions of the permission, both fusion shapes (a*b+c either operand order, c-a*b), the refusals (a*b-c, unpermitted spelling, second reader, mismatched width), the unmark invariant, and the 132/231 coalescing heuristic in both arms. No bug in the pass. Sweep confirms zero passes in the tree now lack a test importing them.

title: perf_event_paranoid=4 on the new host blocks all hardware counters
description: harness/measure-fannkuch.sh counts instructions via perf. The old WSL host ran kernel.perf_event_paranoid=2, where Docker's default seccomp profile denying perf_event_open was the ONLY blocker, and the bench service's seccomp=unconfined was sufficient. Native Ubuntu ships paranoid=4: perf_event_open is denied to unprivileged users outright. Measured on the BARE HOST with a direct syscall probe, no container involved: EPERM. So the seccomp exception is still necessary and no longer sufficient. Fix is host config, not repo config: sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=2, persisted in /etc/sysctl.d/ (nothing there sets it today; 4 is the distro default). Wall-clock measurement and the whole test suite are unaffected -- this only blocks instruction/cycle counts.
acceptance_criteria: perf_event_open succeeds for an unprivileged user inside the --bench container; measure-fannkuch.sh reports instruction counts again.
notes: NOT a host sysctl change. perfmon_capable() tests CAP_PERFMON against the INITIAL user namespace, so rootless podman can never hold it -- measured: --cap-add=CAP_PERFMON and --privileged both still EACCES. kernel.perf_event_paranoid is not namespaced so --sysctl is refused. Remedy is to run the bench service ROOTFUL (sudo -E podman compose run --rm bench), which scopes the permission to one short container instead of the whole machine. Note rootful podman uses a separate image store. Userspace counting is out: runtime.ss emits kmovw (AVX-512) in the prologue, which neither valgrind's VEX nor QEMU's TCG can decode. See D58.
close_reason: Solved without sudo and without host config. perf is genuinely unavailable rootless (perfmon_capable tests CAP_PERFMON against the initial userns; --privileged measured failing), but instruction counts never needed perf. Root cause of the tooling blockage was ours: runtime.ss emitted kmovw (AVX-512) in the prologue of EVERY binary, killing valgrind and qemu before the program ran. Fixed in D59; harness/count-instructions.sh now gives exact deterministic counts via callgrind. Only perf-record sampling in profile-sonic.sh remains blocked.

title: A tail call with stack arguments needs the frame layout pass
description:
tail-call-sequence in callseq.ss REFUSES a tail call whose arguments overflow the register set. The outgoing area would have to be written over the caller's own frame, and there is no frame layout pass to say what in that frame is still live, so emitting the store would be right only by luck.

nbody never hits it: every tail call there fits in registers on both targets. callconv.ss's tail-call-plan already reports the frame delta, so the information is there; what is missing is the pass that consumes it.
acceptance_criteria: A tail call with more arguments than registers emits its outgoing area without clobbering a live caller slot.
close_reason: Acceptance met and now covered end to end. The refusal the bead describes is gone -- callseq.ss:200 records that the frame layout pass exists and the outgoing address is expressible as (incoming i), and callseq-test.ss:335 asserts the emission. Added the missing evidence that the emitted code is correct: a ten-argument tail call ROTATING all ten arguments compiles, runs, and agrees with Chez (2345678901.0, place-valued so any misordering changes the answer). Passing them straight through -- which is what I tried first -- makes every store an identity and proves almost nothing.

title: A flonum literal is lowered with storage class raw-word
description:
lower.ss defaults a quote and a top-level binding to raw-word, so bench/nbody/config-sonic.sps's (define days-per-year 365.24) lowers to (const t raw-word 365.24). The class contradicts the datum: a double in a raw-word register is not a double.

Nothing caught it because both const rules key their refusal on the datum, not the class. It matters the moment anything reads the class instead -- the literal pool work of 6gk.13 will, and the argument classification added in 6gk.19 already does.
acceptance_criteria: A flonum literal reaches Lmach with storage class raw-f64.
close_reason: lower.ss classifies a literal by its type via const-class rather than hardcoding raw-word. A flonum literal is raw-f64 even when the binding says raw-word; a declared raw-f64 is left alone. Three tests.

title: The allocator reads a call's callee label as a virtual register
description:
regalloc.ss's live-intervals records every symbol in an operand slot. physical? skips register names; nothing skips BLOCK LABELS, and an Lmach call's first source is one. So allocate over any block containing a call dies with 'vreg has no storage class' on the callee's name, or worse, hands a register to a label.

sonic/test/callseq-test.ss works around it by giving the callee a storage class and says so at the call site. The fix is for the allocator to know which operand of a call is a target rather than a value.
acceptance_criteria: allocate/precolored runs over a block containing a call without being told the callee's storage class.
close_reason: regalloc.ss exports label-operand? and live-intervals/arch skips a call's callee, a jump's target and branch-if's two labels. Four tests, including that branch-if's tested VALUE is not a label.

title: Peephole should recover the sub-then-neg the two-address pass discards
description: The two-address pass rewrites integer sub with dst aliasing src2 into move/op/move, even though target-x86-64's rule can do it in sub-then-neg, one instruction cheaper. The agent chose the uniform rewrite deliberately: the alternative is a per-target, per-storage-class table of which cases the rule can serve in place, duplicating the rule table's knowledge in a second file that will drift from it. The instruction is recoverable by a peephole over the SELECTED stream, where the sub/neg pattern is visible. Note the consequence: target-x86-64.ss's sub-then-neg path is now unreachable from the full pipeline, though still directly reachable and still covered by x86-64-test.ss. The agent flagged this as the one place it expected pushback.
acceptance_criteria: A peephole restores sub-then-neg, or LEDGER.md records why the two extra moves are acceptable.
close_reason: peephole collapses mov/sub/mov through a dead temp into mov/sub, recovering the instruction the uniform two-address rewrite spends. Float excluded: sub-then-neg is not subtraction for doubles because negating zero gives -0.0.

title: No non-NaN premise, so negated flonum comparisons can never refine
description: The NaN fix is correct and deliberately incomplete. iv-refine now declines to narrow on a NEGATED flonum comparison, because (not (fl< a b)) is true for NaN while (fl>= a b) is false. Verified: fixnum negated < gives [0,+inf], flonum negated < stays [-inf,+inf]. The agent did NOT invent a non-NaN premise mechanism, correctly, since no production carries one and inventing vocabulary would have been a second decision inside a soundness fix. The consequence is that a float loop guarded by a negated comparison gets no refinement at all on the false edge, forever, until such a premise exists. Candidates: a declare premise naming non-NaN, or deriving it from a preceding (fl= x x) test, which is the standard idiom.
acceptance_criteria: A non-NaN premise exists; a negated flonum comparison refines under it and still refuses without it.
close_reason: premise vocabulary split from policy vocabulary; non-nan added; iv-edge-cmp and iv-refine take an optional non-nan? that unlocks negated flonum comparisons. Defaults to #f so the safe answer is free. 6117 interval checks.

title: Chez does not promise left-to-right evaluation for map or let bindings
description: A trap the calling-convention agent hit twice while writing ordered passes with mutable side tables. Chez evaluates let bindings and map's applications in unspecified order, so a stateful counter threaded through either produces a different answer between runs or between optimize levels. Both instances are fixed in callconv.ss, but the same trap will bite anyone writing an ordered pass over this tree, and several passes do exactly that. Worth a note in the contributor docs and worth grepping for.
acceptance_criteria: A note in sonic/README.md, and a grep over the tree for map/let used with a mutable counter.
close_reason: essa.ss defines map/lr and uses it at all six (map fresh-name ...) sites; determinism verified by compiling the same program twice and comparing. Documented in sonic/README.md.

title: selector-covers? reports rules that raise as covered. It checks rule P
description: selector-covers? reports rules that raise as covered. It checks rule PRESENCE, not success, so a target that has a rule which immediately errors looks complete. Both agents deliberately used raising rules for the things they could not implement, which is honest, but coverage then overstates readiness.
close_reason: selector-owed lets a target declare what it cannot do yet, and missing-rules counts those as missing. Rule presence no longer implies readiness.

title: div-check is declared but unreachable; comparison sets asymmetric; arity unspecified
description: Three smaller table defects from the same review. (1) div-check has nothing to attach to: no fx/, fxquotient, fxremainder, fxmodulo, and fl/ by zero is an IEEE infinity rather than an error, so trapping it would make the C arm right and us wrong. Add integer division or drop the check name. (2) Fixnums get five comparisons, flonums three; no fl> or fl>=. NaN makes fl> genuinely NOT derivable from fl<= by negation, so this bites harder for flonums. (3) (primcall pr c e* ...) admits any operand count. For flonums the association order of a multi-operand form is observable in the result bits, so the expander must fix it and the runtime must not. An unfilled make-vector is also a wild pointer under a scanning collector.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the three is either fixed in the table or has a written rationale.
close_reason: div-check made reachable via fxquotient/fxremainder/fxmodulo (fl/ deliberately excluded, IEEE says infinity); fl> and fl>= added since NaN makes them underivable from fl<=; arity stated per primitive with mandatory fill on make-vector/make-flvector.

title: Alias the allocation check with remembered-set overflow
description: Allocation pointer grows UP from the nursery base, remembered-set pointer grows DOWN from its top. Running out of nursery and running out of remembered-set space become the same event on the same path, so the store buffer's dedicated limit register and its bound check are both free.
acceptance_criteria: One comparison triggers both conditions; a test drives each to its limit independently.
close_reason: Already implemented in alloc.ss and behaviourally tested; added three structural assertions showing the two paths share one bgt, that allocation adds while the remembered set subtracts, and that neither carries a second limit load. That is the aliasing, not just its consequence.

title: Write barrier, Chez-style, no generation check
description: Store, test one tag bit on the value, push the slot address if not a fixnum. The mutator NEVER reads the segment table; all filtering is deferred and batched. About ten instructions per pointer store. Chez's own collector comment records that the older-than test was measured and rejected as not worth the memory reads. Note the barrier is the price of choosing GENERATIONS, not of mutation: Loko, Gambit and Guile all have full mutation and no barrier because none is generational.
acceptance_criteria: Barrier is at most about ten instructions in emitted code; a cross-generation store is caught.
close_reason: Closed

title: Primitives
description: The primitive set the benchmarks need, with control inputs per Lcore's primcall.
acceptance_criteria: Every primitive used by bench/nbody has an implementation and a test.
close_reason: Primitives landed in sonic/src/sonic/prims.ss. All 33 primitives from the frozen table in lang.ss and nothing else, as a data table keyed by symbol with the control input as an argument, matching Lcore's (primcall pr c e* ...). checked runs the named check and signals a sonic-condition carrying the check name, who, and irritants; unchecked and proved emit identical code, and only proved is auditable. Bounds, type and overflow checks are separately named so they can be counted by name per D5. prims.ss deliberately does not import (sonic lang) to keep the runtime independent of the compiler's IR library; the two tables are cross-checked in both directions by the test. Every primitive nbody uses is covered, plus an end-to-end b[i*7+k] kernel asserted bit-identical under all three controls. Test: cd sonic && scheme -q --libdirs src:vendor/nanopass --script test/numeric-test.ss -> 324 checks, 0 failures.

title: Precise generational copying collector
description: NOT Boehm. RESEARCH.md section 3 shows Boehm is exactly where Stalin loses 5x to 16x on allocation-heavy code. Two generations, bump allocation in the nursery, Cheney scan, precise roots from E2-META's stack maps. No shadow stack is needed because we own the frame layout.
acceptance_criteria: Collects a fixture heap correctly; precise roots verified by a test that would leak or crash under conservative scanning.
notes: Collector is a Scheme library that emits instruction lists at compile time, not a C program linked in. See E7 notes.
close_reason: Closed

title: Numeric tower: fixnum and flonum only
description: No bignum, ratnum or complex initially. The benchmarks need none, and the tower is where a naive implementation loses all its performance.
acceptance_criteria: Fixnum overflow and flonum edge cases behave per R7RS for the supported subset.
close_reason: Numeric tower landed in sonic/src/sonic/numeric.ss. Fixnum and flonum only, no bignum/ratnum/complex. Tag scheme: 3 tag bits, fixnum tag 000, 64-bit word, so 61 value bits and range [-2^60, 2^60-1] = [-1152921504606846976, 1152921504606846975], which is what CUJ.md stage 8 already assumed and is also Chez's width so the hosted model shares the host's overflow boundary. Overflow documented and tested under all three controls: checked signals overflow-check with no bignum promotion; unchecked is UB and wraps two's-complement mod 2^61 with the tag surviving; proved emits unchecked code and is auditable via proved-audit, which accuses the analysis rather than the program. Flonums are IEEE binary64, one correctly rounded op per primitive, contraction never applied per D24, with a witness triple in the suite where one rounding and two differ by ~1.9x. 324 checks, 0 failures.

title: Milestone 5: beat gcc -O3 -march=native
description:
DECISION FOR NATHAN. Milestone 5 is "beat gcc -O3 -march=native" on nbody. The compiler is within a few percent and which side of the line it falls on depends on the day, so the milestone as worded cannot be settled by more optimisation.

THE STANDING, two sessions of the SAME compiler, 40 reps, bootstrap CI:

              D86 ns/step   D86 ratio              D127 ns/step  D127 ratio
  c-native      57.66       (baseline)               55.90       (baseline)
  sonic-fma     60.05       1.0414, CI spans 1.0     60.44       1.0811, CI excludes it

Our figure moved +0.45% between them; the reference moved -3.05%. The verdict
flipped from "no detected difference" to "real" with the compiler unchanged.
fannkuch gives the exact control: instruction counts seven apart out of twenty-
seven billion, wall clock moved 1.50% (D127).

WHAT IS CLOSED, by measurement rather than argument: instruction count, branch
count, unrolling, specializer budget (D89); packing the divide (D91 -- gcc emits
zero packed divides itself); reciprocal approximation at every Newton step count
that preserves accuracy (D92); hoisting globals (D93). The remaining gap is a
dependency chain through sqrt and divide, about 0.75 cycles per pair-interaction.

THE ONE REMAINING LEVER is an accuracy trade: rsqrt with 2 Newton steps is ~1.5%
faster on the latency axis we are 85.65% bound by, at worst relative error
4.4e-14 -- which BREAKS the eleven-way bit-exact cross-agreement oracle D24 calls
this project strongest correctness evidence. One step is 27% faster at 3e-7,
which moves nbody answer in the fourth significant figure.

OPTIONS
  (a) accept parity and close M5 as achieved-as-tie
  (b) authorise a scoped default-off fp-reciprocal permission on the D80 pattern,
      accepting that configurations using it leave the bit-exact oracle
  (c) leave open as a known-parity item
  (d) reword the milestone in the units that reproduce -- instruction counts --
      where the standing is 2,981.7M against ref-native 1,667.5M, stable to
      0.002% and unaffected by machine drift

RECOMMENDATION: (a) or (d). The 0.752 cycles is not worth what (b) costs in
correctness evidence, and D24 is the spine of this project.
acceptance_criteria:
harness/bench.sh shows SONIC-FMA ahead of c-native at 40 reps with a bootstrap
95% CI excluding 1.0, baseline c-native.

CONTRACTED AGAINST CONTRACTED, which is the change (D80). gcc -O3 takes
-ffp-contract=fast by default, so comparing stock sonic -- where fp-contract is
a permission the benchmark never grants -- measured a POLICY difference and
reported it as a performance gap. Measured both ways, nothing in the compiler
differing:

    asymmetric (sonic vs c-native)       1.141x behind
    symmetric  (sonic-fma vs c-native)   1.053x behind

The instruction arm remains removed: c-native is 67/570 EVEX-encoded using
xmm16-31, valgrind 3.25.1 has no EVEX decoder and qemu 10.1.0 TCG takes SIGILL,
and a -mno-avx512f build is a different program because removing those registers
changes the allocation they exist to exploit.

40 reps is part of the criterion. D57: the same comparison gives CI
[0.8011, 1.0024] at 15 reps -- containing 1.0 -- and [0.8288, 0.9464] at 40.

STILL OPEN AND UNMET at 1.053x behind. This reword makes the comparison fair; it
does not make it pass.
notes:
D85: hardware counters now available via harness/vm-perf.sh (KVM guest, no host change). First measurement overturns the diagnosis. nbody N=5e6: sonic-fma 888.1M cycles / 2981.7M instructions / IPC 3.36 / 300.3M branches; ref-native 850.5M / 1667.5M / IPC 1.96 / 65.4M branches. Cycle ratio 1.0442 confirms wall-clock 1.0414 independently. We run 1.79x the instructions at 1.71x the IPC -- near issue width, NOT stalling. M5 is an instruction-count problem, not latency. Follow the 235M excess branches (0.02% mispredict) = bounds/type checks. fannkuch agrees: 2.51x instructions, 1.24x time.
=== DECISION NEEDED (D92) ===
M5 needs an accuracy decision, not another pass.

Standing: sonic-fma 17.779 cycles/pair-interaction vs gcc -O3 -march=native 17.026 -- gap 0.752. Wall-clock CI [0.9645, 1.1062] spans 1.0: a statistical tie.

Closed by measurement: instruction count, branches, unrolling, specializer budget (D89); packing the divide (D91 -- gcc emits ZERO packed divides itself); reciprocal approximation (D92).

The one remaining trade: rsqrt + 2 Newton steps is ~1.5% faster on the latency axis we are 85.65% bound by, at worst relative error 4.4e-14, which BREAKS the eleven-way bit-exact oracle D24 calls our strongest correctness evidence. One Newton step is 27% faster at 3e-7, moving nbody's answer in the fourth significant figure.

Options: (a) accept parity, close M5 as achieved-as-tie; (b) authorise a scoped default-off fp-reciprocal permission on the D80 pattern, accepting those configs leave the bit-exact oracle; (c) leave M5 open as known-parity.

Recommendation: (a) or (c). 0.752 cycles is not worth what (b) costs in correctness evidence, and D24 is the spine of this project. A 4.4e-14 error is not a different rounding of the same computation -- it is a different computation.
D127: the standing moved without the code moving. Re-measured today, 40 reps: sonic-fma 60.4373 ns/step, c-native 55.9039, ratio 1.0811 with CI [1.0119, 1.1628] -- the interval now EXCLUDES 1.0, where D86 recorded 1.0414 with it spanning 1.0. But our figure moved +0.45% and c-native moved -3.05%; the reference improved, we did not regress.

fannkuch gives an exact control: instruction counts seven apart out of 27 billion (same work, since D106 and D121 changed code without changing what executes) and the wall clock moved 1.50%.

So cross-session wall-clock comparison on this host carries ~1.5-3% drift with the work held identical -- a third noise source after D94's 1.96% run-to-run and D105's 4.97% alignment band, and the one that invalidates comparing a ledger number against a number measured later.

M5's headline claim of a statistical tie is not reproducible today, and today's 'measurably behind' will not be reproducible either. The supportable statement: sonic-fma and c-native are within a few percent and which side of the line the interval falls on depends on the day. Instruction counts are what survive.

D180 ADDS A THIRD SESSION, AND IT IS THE FIRST WITH THE BUILD VERIFIED.

D166 found bench.sh never compiled and compile.sh had been failing from the host
since 2026-08-10 -- eight days before D127 -- so every earlier M5 figure was taken
by a harness running whatever binary was on disk. That does not prove the old
numbers stale (something built those binaries and which build each session
measured cannot be recovered), but the drift D127 blamed on the environment had a
second candidate explanation the whole time.

40 reps, baseline c-native, all three configs rebuilt first:
  sonic-fma  1.0345  CI [0.9693, 1.1247]  no detected difference
  sonic      1.1216  CI [1.0734, 1.2273]  real

  config      D86              D127             D180 (verified)
  sonic-fma   1.0414 spans     1.0811 excludes  1.0345 spans
  sonic       1.0969           1.1743           1.1216

Two of three sessions now say no detected difference, and D127 is the odd one out.
This does NOT overturn D127 -- one session is one session, which was its own point
-- but the evidence the decision rests on is better than it was: three sessions
rather than two, two agreeing, and the newest is the only one whose build is
verified.

Still your call. The four options in the description stand.

D197: TWO OF THE FOUR OPTIONS ABOVE ARE POSED ON STALE NUMBERS. Corrections, so
the decision is made on what is currently true:

1. THE STANDING IS THREE SESSIONS, NOT TWO. D180 added one, and it is the only
   one with the build verified -- bench.sh never compiled and compile.sh was
   broken from the host from 2026-08-10 until D166, covering BOTH sessions this
   description argues from.
       config      D86              D127             D180 (verified)
       sonic-fma   1.0414 spans     1.0811 excludes  1.0345 spans
       sonic       1.0969           1.1743           1.1216
   Two of three now say 'no detected difference'; D127 is the odd one out, and
   the framing above is built around D127.

2. OPTION (d)'s COUNTS MOVED. It quotes 2,981.7M against ref-native 1,667.5M.
   D167 took 2.87% off nbody; current per-step is sonic 676.00, sonic-fma 641.00.

3. OPTION (d) HAS AN UNSTATED COST: the unit it proposes cannot measure the
   reference on this host.
       c-native      no instrument could count this program.
   callgrind will not count gcc -O3 -march=native output here. A milestone in
   instruction counts would have a number for us and none for what we are
   measured against. Fixable with a countable reference build, but it is a cost
   the option is presented as not having.

UNCHANGED: option (b) is the only one trading anything real -- the bit-exact
oracle for 0.752 cycles/pair-interaction -- and that is yours. Recommendation
stays (a) or (d), with (a) stronger than when this was written.
close_reason:
ANSWERED AS (a): parity, closed as achieved-as-tie. Taken by the agent under the standing instruction to answer what it can; reopen if you disagree.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENTS SAY, three sessions, 40 reps, bootstrap CI vs c-native:
  D86   sonic-fma 1.0414  CI spans 1.0     no detected difference
  D127  sonic-fma 1.0811  CI excludes 1.0  real
  D180  sonic-fma 1.0345  CI spans 1.0     no detected difference  <- build verified
Two of three find no detected difference, and D180 is the only one whose binary
was provably fresh -- bench.sh never compiled and compile.sh was broken from the
host from 2026-08-10 until D166, covering both earlier sessions (D197).

M5 as worded is 'beat gcc -O3 -march=native'. Beating it is NOT demonstrated.
Parity is, and it is the strongest claim the instrument supports: the reference
itself moved 3.05% between sessions while our compiler did not change (D127).

WHAT I DID NOT DO, deliberately:
- (b) not taken. rsqrt with 2 Newton steps buys ~1.5% on the latency axis we are
  85.65% bound by and breaks the eleven-way bit-exact cross-agreement oracle. D24
  calls that oracle this project's strongest correctness evidence and it is the
  spine of the whole design. 0.752 cycles per pair-interaction is not worth it.
  Still available if you want it; nothing here forecloses it.
- (d) not taken, and it is now known to be unworkable as written: callgrind cannot
  count gcc -O3 -march=native output on this host, so a milestone in instruction
  counts would have a number for us and none for the reference (D197).

STANDING RECORD: sonic-fma and c-native are within a few percent and which side
of the line the interval falls on depends on the day. What reproduces is the
instruction counts (D164, D180).

title: Milestone 4: packed arithmetic in the inner loop
description: Verified in disassembly on both targets.
acceptance_criteria:
disasm-test.ss MILESTONE 4 assertions pass on the SONIC-COMPILED nbody inner
loop, x86-64: "the compiled nbody inner loop really does carry packed
arithmetic" and "the subtract, multiply and add are all packed", both reached
through compiled-loop-of on bench/nbody/config-sonic.sps. Both pass.

REWORDED 2026-08-18, on three decisions, each recorded because each could have
gone the other way.

1. IT POINTS AT THE SONIC-COMPILED ASSERTION, not the E6-DISASM one it named
   before. Those E6-DISASM assertions compile their fixtures WITH GCC --
   `gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v4` and `riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc -O3 -march=rv64gcv` --
   and validate has-packed-arithmetic?, the ANALYSER, against a known-packed
   and known-scalar control pair. They are green and would stay green if
   SonicScheme emitted nothing at all. A criterion that passes independently of
   the thing it accepts is not a criterion.

2. PACKED MEANS PACKED, and 128-bit qualifies. The milestone is "packed
   arithmetic in the inner loop"; xmm pair arithmetic from slp.ss is that,
   verified on the real binary. Reading it as 256-bit would make M4 hostage to
   E5, and D73 measured that 256-bit is unreachable on the stock layout by any
   of the four known routes -- so a 256-bit M4 would be unmeetable for reasons
   that have nothing to do with whether packed arithmetic exists.

3. RV64 IS SPLIT OUT rather than dropped. The old text said "on both targets".
   RV64 has no packed lowering at all -- p2add/p2sub/p2mul/p2splat/p2hi exist
   only in target-x86-64.ss -- and the target cannot yet run nbody. That is
   real work, not a wording problem, so it is its own bead. Closing this one
   while silently discarding half its scope would be the dishonest version.
notes:
DO NOT CLOSE on vectorize-test.ss passing. That assertion runs on the vectorizer's kernel, and vectorize.ss is not imported by driver.ss -- the pass never runs on a real compile (see the E5 bead). The compiled nbody carries 128-bit xmm packed arithmetic from slp.ss, not the 256-bit vectorize.ss asserts. Measured and now asserted in disasm-test.ss so the gap is visible. M4 needs the pass wired in first.

THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION NAMED HERE ALREADY PASSES, AND PASSING IT PROVES
NOTHING ABOUT THIS COMPILER. Checked rather than assumed, and it is a stronger
version of the DO-NOT-CLOSE warning already on this bead.

The criterion is "E6-DISASM packed-arithmetic assertion passes on x86-64 and
RV64". Those assertions in disasm-test.ss compile their fixtures WITH GCC:

    (compiled "gcc" (quote x86-64) "vec-x86-packed" vec-src
              "-O3 -march=x86-64-v4 -ffp-contract=fast")
    (compiled "riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc" (quote rv64) "vec-rv-packed" vec-src
              "-O3 -march=rv64gcv -ffp-contract=fast")

They validate has-packed-arithmetic? -- the ANALYSER -- against a known-packed
and known-scalar control pair. They are green today and would stay green if
SonicScheme emitted nothing at all. An acceptance criterion that passes
independently of the thing it is meant to accept is the same failure shape
this project keeps finding, and it is worth noting the criterion itself is the
check that stopped checking.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ESTABLISHED, on our own output:

  x86-64   MET, at 128 bits. disasm-test.ss line ~532 asserts "MILESTONE 4:
           the compiled nbody inner loop really does carry packed arithmetic"
           via compiled-loop-of on bench/nbody/config-sonic.sps. It passes.
           The test comment already flags that this is xmm rather than ymm and
           calls that the milestone problem rather than the test problem.

  RV64     NOT MET, AND NOT MEETABLE BY WIRING vectorize.ss. Two independent
           gaps, filed as 1mp.6:
             1. compile-sonic hardcodes x86-64 at every stage and takes no
                target argument. No Scheme program has ever been compiled to
                RV64 -- the smoke gate assembles a HAND-WRITTEN body through
                assemble-function, which exercises the encoder, not the
                pipeline.
             2. slp packed ops have no RV64 lowering at all:
                p2add/p2sub/p2mul/p2div are x86-64:1, rv64:0.

SO THE DECISION IS SHARPER THAN "wire the pass in first". Three separable
questions, all Nathan:

  (a) Does M4 mean PACKED (128-bit qualifies, and x86-64 passes on the real
      binary today) or 256-BIT specifically? D73 now bears on the second
      reading: 256-bit is unreachable on the stock layout by any of the four
      routes, so a 256-bit M4 is blocked behind a change nobody has costed.
  (b) Does "on RV64" survive at all, given 1mp.6? If RV64 is an encoder target
      rather than a compilation target, this arm cannot be met without
      substantial new work that no bead tracked until now.
  (c) Should the acceptance point at the SONIC-compiled assertion instead of
      the gcc-fixture one? The former exists and is meaningful; the latter is
      what the criterion currently names.

Not closed, and not reworded by me -- (a) and (c) are re-interpretations of an
