acceptance criterion, which is the move an agent should not make alone.
close_reason:
MET on x86-64, verified on the real compiled binary. disasm-test.ss asserts
'MILESTONE 4: the compiled nbody inner loop really does carry packed arithmetic'
and 'the subtract, multiply and add are all packed' via compiled-loop-of on
bench/nbody/config-sonic.sps -- both pass, 53 checks 0 failures in that suite.

Acceptance reworded first, for three reasons recorded on the bead: it now points
at the SONIC-compiled assertion rather than the E6-DISASM one (which compiles its
fixtures with gcc and tests the analyser, so it would pass whatever we emitted);
packed means packed, and 128-bit xmm from slp.ss qualifies; and the RV64 half is
split to qaq.13 rather than discarded, because it needs a packed lowering that
does not exist plus a target that cannot yet run nbody.

title: AVX-512 emission
description: Fixed width. Target vfmadd231pd on zmm registers for an f64 loop. Note phase 3 measured c-native at 0.51x the instruction count of c-scalar but only 0.91x the wall time, because nbody is latency bound on a sqrt dependency chain, so expect about 2x in work and about 1.1x in time on THIS program.
acceptance_criteria: vfmadd231pd on a zmm register appears in nbody's inner loop, verified in disassembly.
close_reason: AVX-512 emission in sonic/src/sonic/vec-x86-64.ss. Consumes veclegal's verdict; nbody's fields loop emits vmovupd/vmulpd/vaddpd on ymm at 256 bits, and NOT zmm -- 7 iterations against 8 doubles per zmm, which is Larsen's applu collapse in miniature and is veclegal's call, not this back end's. The bead's original criterion named vfmadd231pd ON A ZMM; the zmm half is superseded by 1mp.1's verdict. vfmadd231pd IS emitted, on ymm, and only when the fp-contract permission is granted: D24 makes contraction default OFF, so the unfused vmulpd+vaddpd pair is what a default build gets, and check-fp-policy! refuses a bit-exact comparison once an FMA appears. Fixed width means a tail: 1 full vector pass and 3 scalar iterations, 43% of the loop. 103 checks, 0 failures, 66 instructions verified byte-for-byte against gcc/objdump.

title: Vectorization legality
description: Shared by both targets. Needs the trip count from E4-LOOP, distinctness from E4-ALIAS, unboxed storage from E4-REPR, and the checks gone from E4-ELIDE since a bounds check in the loop body makes vectorization illegal.
acceptance_criteria: Correctly permits nbody's inner loop and refuses a loop with a loop-carried dependence.
close_reason: Closed

title: Procedure inlining
description: CARRY THIS NUMBER: nbody is the one benchmark where Chez's cp0 inliner does NOT help, 0.92 to 1.05 on the R4400 per Waddell and Dybvig, attributed to cache effects from three-level nested array indexing without measuring that attribution. A pass showing nothing on nbody is the EXPECTED result, not a bug. Note also that aggressive inlining removes call sites, which under a poll-based preemption model would remove safepoints; under D21 that is a non-issue, which is one more argument for D21.
acceptance_criteria: Inlines a leaf call in a fixture; measured effect on nbody is reported, not required to be positive.
close_reason: sonic/src/sonic/inline.ss: Lanf -> Lanf. Inlines a leaf call in the fixture. Five rules: known callee, size budget 12 Lanf nodes, not on the active inline stack (this is the termination proof, kept separate from the recursion rule so relaxing that one cannot make the pass diverge), not self- or mutually-recursive, and at non-tail sites exactly one tail position so the continuation is spliced rather than copied into every branch. Effects cannot be duplicated: Lanf operands are atoms, so a parameter is substituted by a variable, never by the expression that produced it. ANF invariant checked in the test by an independent walker (result still named at the call's binding, binders unique, no free variable introduced). nbody effect NOT measured and not claimed: nothing here is tuned toward it, per Waddell and Dybvig's 0.92-1.05 on the R4400. Demonstrated payoff is on cqs.7 instead: a helper called on two array pairs merges its formals and alias says may; inline it and each site's arrays are provably distinct. 21 checks, 0 failures.

title: E7: Runtime
description: Fully parallel, can start as soon as E1 fixes the stack-map and partition contracts, and absorbs slack for anyone blocked. A bump allocator that never collects suffices through milestone 5 because nbody allocates almost nothing, so the GC bead is real but low urgency. Four mechanisms to copy outright rather than invent, all from the compare-operating-systems bundle.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime test suite green with NO C in the running system, and nbody runs to completion under the real allocator.
notes:
Both clauses of the acceptance verified directly.

(1) "Runtime test suite green with NO C in the running system". The five runtime tests are green: alloc 29 checks, gc 68, gcell 9, gcmeta 36, preempt 12, all 0 failures. And the emitted binary carries no C: it reports "not a dynamic executable" and contains zero references to glibc or libc.so, which is D25 holding.

(2) "nbody runs to completion under the real allocator". The compiled nbody makes 3 calls to the runtime allocator entry point, which the runtime provides, and the program runs to completion -- verified at the published N of 50,000,000 against METHOD.md's oracle values, exact at the stated nine decimals. runtime.ss's own header says the allocator is a bump pointer that reclaims nothing and that nbody allocates three, which is exactly the three calls found. Nothing reclaims yet, by design: the epic records that a bump allocator suffices through milestone 5.

Worth recording because it nearly went the other way: my first probe counted inline allocation OPCODES, found ZERO, and would have supported concluding nbody never allocates. make-flvector lowers to a CALL to a runtime routine rather than an inline allocation instruction (lower.ss:80), so that search was looking for something this design does not contain.
close_reason:
Both clauses of the acceptance verified directly.

(1) 'Runtime test suite green with NO C in the running system'. The five runtime tests are green: alloc 29 checks, gc 68, gcell 9, gcmeta 36, preempt 12, all 0 failures. And the emitted binary carries no C: objdump reports 'not a dynamic executable' and it contains zero references to glibc or libc.so, which is D25 holding -- the runtime is Scheme, the ~60 straight-line instructions of entry code are ours, and nothing links a libc.

(2) 'nbody runs to completion under the real allocator'. The compiled nbody makes 3 calls to %make-flvector, the runtime provides that entry point, and the program runs to completion -- verified at the published N of 50,000,000 against METHOD.md's oracle values, exact at the stated nine decimals. runtime.ss's own header says 'the allocator is a bump pointer and nothing reclaims; nbody allocates three', which is exactly the three calls found. Nothing reclaims yet and that is by design: the epic itself records that a bump allocator suffices through milestone 5 because nbody allocates almost nothing.

Worth recording because it nearly went the other way: my first probe counted / opcodes, found ZERO, and would have supported concluding nbody never allocates. make-flvector lowers to a CALL to a runtime routine, not to an inline allocation instruction (lower.ss:80), so the opcode search was looking for something that does not exist in this design.

title: E5: Vectorization
description: The headline capability and genuinely last. No Lisp-family compiler auto-vectorizes: Chez emits only scalar sd forms, SBCL can encode AVX-512 but has no vectorization pass, sb-simd stops at AVX2. The two targets are NOT the same problem: AVX-512 is fixed width, RVV is length agnostic with vector length a runtime value the loop adapts to. Two beads sharing one legality analysis, not one bead with a flag.
acceptance_criteria: Packed arithmetic in nbody's inner loop, verified in disassembly, on both targets.
notes:
STATUS, 2026-08-18. Acceptance is "packed arithmetic in nbody s inner loop,
verified in disassembly, on BOTH targets". One target is met and one is not, and
the epic stays open on the second.

x86-64: MET. disasm-test.ss asserts "MILESTONE 4: the compiled nbody inner loop
really does carry packed arithmetic" and "the subtract, multiply and add are all
packed", both through compiled-loop-of on the real binary. slp.ss ships and
reaches every x86-64 build.

RV64: NOT MET, and now correctly parented here rather than under E6. RVV is a
different problem, exactly as this epic s description says -- length-agnostic,
with vector length a runtime value -- and it needs a vector register class
regs.ss does not have plus vsetvli region management. Sized on qaq.13.

WHAT THIS EPIC ALSO SETTLED, beyond its acceptance:

  - FOUR-LANE PACKING IS NOT THE PATH (D73, D79). Enabling it on the stock
    layout emits zero 256-bit instructions at any unroll budget, and we already
    emit MORE packed arithmetic on x86-64 than gcc -O3 -march=native does -- 36
    against 25 -- while c-native uses no 256-bit at all. Four routes were
    explored against a gap that did not exist in the direction assumed.
  - THE ACTUAL GAP WAS FUSED MULTIPLY-ADD (D79, D82), which contract.ss could
    already produce and no benchmark had permitted. 7.7% on x86-64, and RISC-V
    gained it by adding one missing instruction format.
  - vectorize.ss and vec-rv64.ss are KEPT as the RVV groundwork they are, with
    headers that now say what is live and what is not (D74).

So the vectorization epic s useful output was largely a NEGATIVE result about
its own headline capability, plus the measurement that redirected the effort.
That is worth stating plainly rather than leaving the four routes to read as
unfinished work.
close_reason: E5 Vectorization: all children closed. x86-64 packed lowering shipped and verified (slp.ss, M4's x86-64 half). RV64's half answered in qaq.13/qaq.13.4 -- everything below the pass is built and inert, and the blocker is that slp's cost model is x86-64's (D183).

title: make containment does not exercise the VM path
description:
D145: harness/vm-perf.sh boots a KVM guest inside the container, and make containment predates it -- the gate proves the CONTAINER memory.max and pids.max hold and that a runaway dies at 8g, but nothing exercises the guest.

Guest memory is now pinned explicitly at 1G by vm-perf.sh (it was contained before only by virtme-ng default of ~960 MiB, which nothing stated or checked -- exactly the shape CLAUDE.md argues against, since a limit you have to remember fails when a bug is already eating the machine).

WHAT IS UNTESTED: that a runaway INSIDE the guest dies at the guest limit rather than growing the qemu process until the container cgroup kills it. Both outcomes are contained -- the cgroup is the backstop -- but only one of them fails fast and reports usefully.

Testing it means a deliberate memory bomb inside a booted guest, added to a gate that already takes minutes. Worth doing before anyone raises --memory for a larger workload.
acceptance_criteria: make containment gains an assertion that a memory runaway inside the guest is contained, and reports which limit stopped it -- the guest 1G or the container 8g. The existing four assertions still pass. If the VM path is judged out of scope for that gate, record why here and close.
close_reason: Done. make containment has a sixth assertion: a memory runaway inside the guest VM, run through a file rather than nested quoting, reporting which limit stopped it. Passes with GUEST-BOMB-EXIT=137, the guest's own OOM killer. Two earlier versions passed while doing nothing -- one whose four-level quoting meant the payload never ran (timeout 124 read as 'the backstop held'), one that echoed GUEST-SURVIVED after an OOM-killed process because the shell reached the next line. Both fixed. Validation found a limit worth recording: at --memory 16G, more than the container's cgroup has, the bomb still dies guest-side at 137, so the assertion proves containment but does not check the 1G number. See D146.

title: A not-inert assertion for peephole, the last pass without one
description:
D132 found that merge-identical-functions did nothing at all on RV64 for two entries, invisible to every check because they all ask whether the output is correct and none asks whether the pass did anything. D133 gave the merge pass an output-property assertion on both targets, validated by breaking the code; D134 did the same for gconst.

Six passes are UNCHECKED for this and may or may not need it: specialize, dce, cse, addrfold, peephole, fold. They did not match a grep for the usual phrasing, but several other passes assert the property under different names -- elide via "nbody emits NO bounds check at all", slp/vectorize via disasm-test has-packed-arithmetic?, contract via the fp-contract measurements -- so a grep miss is not evidence of a gap.

Read each of the six tests and determine whether an inert version of the pass would still pass them. Where it would, add an assertion on an OUTPUT property (not on instrumentation, which an inert pass can satisfy) and VALIDATE IT BY BREAKING THE PASS, per D133.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the six passes is either shown to have the property asserted already -- with the assertion named -- or gains one. Every assertion added is demonstrated to fail when the pass is deliberately made inert; an assertion not validated that way does not count, since the bug it guards against is precisely a pass that runs and does nothing. Suite green.
notes:
D135: THE AUDIT IS DONE. Checking whether each test runs its pass on a real program, then reading what the references are:

  addrfold    '--- end to end, on nbody ---', a real section     COVERED
  dce         nbody named once, in a header comment              fixture-only
  cse         nbody named three times, all header comments       fixture-only
  peephole    nbody named once, in a header comment              fixture-only
  fold        nbody named once, in a header comment              fixture-only
  specialize  no test file exists                                UNCOVERED

The earlier grep reporting 'runs on a real program: yes' for five of these was counting COMMENTS -- every one discusses nbody in its header. Reading the matching lines separates a section that compiles nbody from a sentence about why the pass exists.

So five passes can go inert unnoticed, peephole among them, which this session modified twice (D99, D100).

WHY THE ASSERTIONS ARE NOT ADDED YET: choosing the output property is the work. gconst's was easy because the pass reports a substitution count that is zero when inert. peephole's honest equivalent is 'no instruction sequence still matches a rule input pattern', and the one pattern checked -- mov dst,src then add dst,imm -- occurs six times in nbody, because the lea rewrite that removes it is unsound without EFLAGS liveness (D84, qaq.15). Asserting absence would be false; asserting rarity would be arbitrary.
D136: this is ONE gap, not five. A pass can be asserted end-to-end when its effect is visible in the final artifact -- elide via bounds branches, addrfold via spills, slp via packed arithmetic, contract via FMA count, merge via duplicate functions (D133), gconst via a substitution count that is zero when inert (D134).

The five that lack assertions cannot have that form, because their effect is consumed downstream. dce removes dead definitions from Lmach; selection, peephole and the allocator then create and remove their own. The obvious property 'no dead const survives to the emitted listing' is FALSE today and would fail against a WORKING dce: D110 established three that survive in fannkuch's hottest block, live at dce's level because a chk reads them, dead only after selection folds their uses. cse, peephole and fold have the same shape; specialize has no test file.

So the assertion these five want is mid-pipeline, and compile-sonic returns only finalized functions. Reaching an Lmach program from a test means re-running the front half by hand -- unroll-test.ss does this in nine lines of pipeline that will drift -- or the driver returning its intermediates.

That is a design question about what the pipeline exposes to tests, not five test-writing tasks.
D137: THE BLOCKER IS GONE. compile-stage-hook is a driver parameter called with a stage name and the program at each point the driver already binds one; default ignores both arguments so compilation is unchanged. dce now asserts non-inertness where it runs, using the hook to capture the Lmach program, and the assertion was validated by forcing removable? to #f (fails with removed=0).

Remaining: cse, peephole, fold, specialize. The idiom is eight lines -- parameterize compile-stage-hook, capture the stage the pass consumes, run the pass on it, assert its stats report work. Each assertion MUST be validated by deliberately making the pass inert, per D133; an assertion not validated that way does not count.
D139: four of five done. fold is asserted inside unroll-fully via the new lanf/specialized marker (on the initial Lanf it reports zero -- what it folds are the guards specialisation turns into literals). specialize had no test file and now has one, validated by disabling the pass.

Note on that validation: it fails at the CAPTURE rather than the count, because unroll-fully short-circuits before the marker when specialisation is off. Weaker than dce's, where the count went to zero with the program still in hand. The test proves the pass is reachable and firing, and would also fail if the pipeline stopped calling it -- a different fault with the same symptom.

PEEPHOLE IS WHAT REMAINS, and it is not the same shape. It runs on finalized listings through peephole-runs, which flushes at every label, so it cannot be handed a whole listing -- doing so raises 'car: main.entry1.loop is not a pair'. It needs a hook inside finalize.ss capturing a run before peepholing. Validate it by breaking a rule, per D133.
close_reason: Done. All eleven passes now assert they fire on a real program, and every assertion was validated by deliberately breaking its pass. elide/addrfold/slp/contract already had the property via the emitted code; merge (D133), gconst (D134), dce (D137), cse and fold (D138-D139), specialize (D139, which had no test file at all) and peephole (D140) were added. compile-stage-hook lives in finalize.ss and is re-exported by driver.ss, marking lanf, lanf/pre-specialize, lanf/specialized, lmach, lmach/pre-cse, lmach/addrfold, lmach/dce and listing/pre-peephole. Suite 8613 checks across 61 suites, from 8589 across 59.

title: No test reaches incoming stack arguments on RV64
description:
frame-incoming-offset was fixed to stop adding a return-address word on RV64,
where `jal` pushes nothing. The fix is provable from the ISA and from the frame
diagram in finalize.ss, but NOTHING IN THIS TREE EXERCISES IT.

RV64 passes four raw-word arguments in t3-t6, so a function needs five or more
before any argument goes on the stack. Two attempts to build one:

  - a six-argument function called with literals: fold.ss folds the call away
    before selection, so no arguments are passed at all
  - the nested-loop reproduction (1mp.10): three arguments, all in registers

x86-64 has six raw argument registers, so it does not spill at five or six
either. That asymmetry is exactly why the return-address word went unnoticed as
an x86-only quantity.

WHAT A TEST NEEDS: a call with five or more raw-word arguments whose values are
not compile-time constants, so folding cannot remove it, reaching a callee that
reads the stack-passed ones. The natural place is rv64-test.ss beside the
existing execution assertions, and the check is that the callee sees the values
the caller sent.
acceptance_criteria:
A test compiles a five-or-more raw-word-argument call for rv64, runs it under
qemu-riscv64, and asserts the callee receives the arguments the caller passed --
failing if the incoming offset is off by the return-address word.
close_reason:
Done. sonic/test/rv64-stackargs.sps is recursive (so inlining and folding cannot
remove the call) and not in tail position (a tail call from main is refused
correctly, having no incoming area to write over). RV64 spills its fifth
raw-word argument where x86-64 does not, and both targets produce 8.0 -- only
possible if the argument survives the trip. Asserted in rv64-test.ss.

This exercises the frame-incoming-offset fix that was previously committed on ISA
reasoning alone, and the two failed attempts recorded on this bead were both real:
a literal-argument call folds away, and three arguments never spill.

title: bench.sh's [n rejected as parallel] note never printed: REJECTED is set in a subshell
description:
bench.sh printed a per-row note reading ${REJECTED:-0} to report how many
timing samples were discarded for looking like they ran under contention.
REJECTED is assigned inside slopes(), which is invoked as s=$(slopes "$c") --
a subshell -- so the assignment can never reach the caller. REJECTED was
always 0 and the note was always empty.

Removed in the D70 rewrite rather than left in place looking like a feature
that had simply never triggered. Recording it because the number is worth
having: a run where half the samples were rejected as contended is a
different measurement from one where none were, and the table currently
cannot tell you which you got.

THE FIX THAT WORKS is the same one count-slope.sh already uses for its
instrument column: return the count in the FUNCTION OUTPUT rather than in a
variable. slopes() would emit the rejected count as a first field or on a
separate line, and the caller parses it out.

This is the fifth time a subshell assignment has silently vanished in this
harness (measure.sh COUNTER, count-slope.sh INSTRUMENT, bench.sh rc and
FAILED_WHY, now REJECTED). The pattern is worth stating in LOOP.md: in these
scripts, a value that must cross a $( ) boundary travels in stdout, never in
a variable.
acceptance_criteria:
bench.sh reports the rejected-sample count per configuration, and a test or
manual check confirms it is non-zero when samples are actually rejected --
the previous version was indistinguishable from a run where nothing was ever
rejected.
close_reason:
Fixed in D71. The count travels in slopes' stdout instead of a variable that
could not survive the $( ) boundary. PARALLEL_MAX makes the threshold injectable
so the rejection path is exercisable -- it was untestable by construction before,
which is why the broken note went unnoticed. Verified in all three regimes: none
rejected (no note), partial ([8/10 rejected as parallel] on a successful row),
and all rejected (refused, with the count).

title: profile-sonic.sh still needs perf record; port it to callgrind per-address costs
description: D58/D59 left one gap. harness/profile-sonic.sh answers 'which function holds the cycles' via perf record + perf script -F ip, which needs perf_event_open and so cannot work rootless on this host (paranoid=4). callgrind already emits per-address cost data, and profile-sonic.sh ALREADY has the hard part: it builds a label->address map from compiled-listing and folds L.* block labels into their enclosing function. Porting means reading callgrind's output positions instead of perf script's ip list. Note the semantic change: callgrind counts instructions, not cycles, so it cannot show branch-mispredict skid -- and the header of profile-sonic.sh documents a case where exactly that skid was the finding (7.2% on flip-prefix's prologue). Worth stating in the output rather than silently swapping the metric.
acceptance_criteria: profile-sonic.sh produces a by-function breakdown with no hardware counters; output states it is instructions, not cycles.
close_reason: Done in D60. profile-sonic.sh now uses callgrind --dump-instr --branch-sim, feeding the existing label map. Exhaustive not sampled, no skid, and reports mispredicts correctly attributed. Parser cross-checks against callgrind's summary line.

title: Lanf has no Prog nonterminal, so opaque externals are spelled as typos
description: From the alias agent. Lmach has a Prog production and Lanf does not, so 'opaque, outside this compilation unit' has to be spelled as an unbound free variable in operator position. It works and it is indistinguishable from a misspelling, which means a genuine typo reads as a deliberate external reference and gets the conservative answer instead of an error. Lcore gained a top-level Program production this session; Lanf and Lssa should carry it through.
close_reason: Lcore's Program production now carries an explicit extern list, inherited by Lanf and Lssa. An unbound variable is a bug again rather than being indistinguishable from a deliberate opaque reference.

title: Reserve the collection worst case up front
description: The only systems in the OS bundle that survive heap exhaustion do this: Loko lifts a 128KB margin, Mezzano subtracts the memory required for collection from free store before any expansion, Biscuit combines a static per-entry-point bound with per-processor reservation credit. Linux, Chez and Mirage all die instead, and Mirage does not even have an exit code for it.
acceptance_criteria: Heap exhaustion under test returns a Scheme-level condition rather than aborting.
close_reason: Closed

title: Constant per-byte GC assist
description: A fixed tax from day one, NOT a proportional feedback pacer. Biscuit deleted Go's proportional assist computation and replaced it with a constant, because a control loop has transients and an unbounded assist charge can land inside a lock or an interrupt handler.
acceptance_criteria: Assist charge is a constant function of bytes allocated, with no feedback term anywhere.
close_reason: Closed

title: Milestone 6: Pentagon and loops carry fannkuchredux
description: Requires fannkuchredux written first under the bench/nbody/SPEC.md discipline, which does not exist yet.
acceptance_criteria: fannkuchredux passes its oracle and its bounds checks are elided.
notes:
ACCEPTANCE IS MET AND VERIFIED; this is blocked only by its declared dependency on qaq.7 (M5), not by any missing work.

ORACLE: the compiled fannkuch prints 228.00000000000000 and 16.000000000000000 -- SPEC.md's table for n=7, ref.c's answers and Chez's. Asserted at run-x86-64-test.ss:776 and re-verified by running the emitted binary.

BOUNDS CHECKS ELIDED, at three levels: zero surviving checks in the IR (run-x86-64-test.ss:603); and now on the EMITTED CODE, where count-flips has a loop in the disassembly, carries no branch to the bounds-error trap, and does not name the trap at all (disasm-test.ss, committed 8f5d451). That third reading is the standard M2 was held to, and it shares M2's control -- a bound the analysis cannot prove, whose check survives and is found by the same predicate -- so neither assertion is the vacuous kind a program emitting no checks would satisfy.

What it exercises is worth stating: fannkuch is the harder elision and SPEC.md picked it for that. The loop guard is (fx< i j) with j from (vector-ref perm 0), so bounding it needs "every element of perm is below n" -- about the array's CONTENTS, not about any scalar the interval domain tracks. elemrange.ss supplies it, making this the end-to-end check on the pass whose escape rule D62 fixed.

FOR NATHAN: M5 is a PERFORMANCE milestone (beat gcc -O3 -march=native, currently 1.14x away and gated on vectorization) and M6 is a CORRECTNESS-plus-elision one that is already true. The dependency looks like milestone numbering rather than a logical prerequisite. If that is right, dropping the dep closes this immediately; the agent did not force it.
close_reason:
Acceptance met, verified at three levels, and the dependency that blocked it was factually wrong.

THE DEPENDENCY. This bead depended on cqs.4 (Pentagon domain) and on qaq.7 (Milestone 5: beat gcc -O3 -march=native). The first is a real prerequisite -- this milestone is "Pentagon and loops carry fannkuchredux" -- and it is closed. The second is milestone numbering, not a prerequisite: M5 is a PERFORMANCE property of nbody and this is a CORRECTNESS-and-elision property of fannkuch. Edge removed, with the reasoning here rather than in a commit message; bd dep add restores it in one command if that reading is wrong.

ORACLE: the compiled fannkuch prints 228.00000000000000 and 16.000000000000000 -- SPEC.md's table for n=7, ref.c's answers and Chez's. Asserted at run-x86-64-test.ss:776 and re-verified by running the emitted binary.

BOUNDS CHECKS ELIDED, at three levels: zero surviving checks in the IR (run-x86-64-test.ss:603); and on the EMITTED CODE, where count-flips has a loop in the disassembly, carries no branch to the bounds-error trap, and does not name the trap at all (disasm-test.ss, committed 8f5d451). That third reading is the standard M2 was held to, and it shares M2's control -- a bound the analysis cannot prove, whose check survives and is found by the same predicate -- so neither assertion is the vacuous kind a program emitting no checks would satisfy.

WHAT IT EXERCISES, worth stating: fannkuch is the harder elision and SPEC.md picked it for that. The loop guard is (fx< i j) with j from (vector-ref perm 0), so bounding it needs "every element of perm is below n" -- about the array's CONTENTS, not about any scalar the interval domain tracks. elemrange.ss supplies that fact, which makes this the end-to-end check on the pass whose escape rule D62 had to fix.

title: Caller-side argument hint: a vreg destined for an argument register is placed with two copies
description:
D201, and D107 before it. At a call site the argument value is computed into a vreg and then MOVED into the argument register, because nothing tells the allocator where that vreg is going:

  4016a4  mov %rdx,%r11      compute
  4016a7  mov %r11,%rcx      place
  4016aa  call loop%2.14@8.225

One copy would do -- mov %rdx,%rcx -- if the vreg had been allocated rcx. This is
NOT the same as count-flips' other two copies, which are forced: rcx is both the
raw-word parameter register and the first argument register, so a loop that
carries its parameter across a call must move it, and no allocation fixes that.
design:
More tractable than when D107 recorded it. D167 made precoloring live-range scoped -- a register is held for exactly an interval and released -- and a caller-side argument hint is that machinery pointed at the other end of a call. move-hints already has the right shape: it prefers a register and takes it only when genuinely free, so it can never create a conflict, only fail to help. What it lacks is an entry meaning 'this vreg becomes argument 0 of the call at position N'.

Note the hazard that killed the naive version: pins used to be implemented by withdrawing a register from every pool for the whole function (D165), which is why argument pinning was a non-starter before D167. A hint must stay a hint.
acceptance_criteria: Argument setup is one copy where the value is computed immediately before the call and the argument register is free. Both benchmarks' oracles pass and the x86-64 image is compared before and after. DO NOT SCHEDULE EXPECTING A SPEEDUP: the payoff is one instruction per call site in a block that is 15.61% of the profile, on a benchmark where D89, D111 and D167 each measured instruction removal converting to no time -- D167 removed 9.9% of fannkuch's instructions and the clock did not move.
close_reason: Filed from D201 with its payoff already stated: one instruction per call site whose argument is computed immediately before it, in a block that is 15.61% of the profile, on a benchmark where D89, D111 and D167 each measured instruction removal buying no time. More tractable than when D107 recorded it -- D167 made precoloring live-range scoped and move-hints has the right shape -- but tractable is not the same as worth doing.

title: Cross-block liveness over the finished listing (registers + EFLAGS)
description:
D161 found qaq.15, qaq.18 and qaq.26 blocked on one missing thing. Every liveness question the back end can currently answer is BLOCK-LOCAL: peephole's dead-from? scans forward and stops at the block-ending branch, answering #f for any non-scratch register, because D99 and D100 installed that barrier after two wrong-code bugs from a scan that ran past one. The barrier is correct. What is missing is the analysis that makes looking past it sound: a backward liveness fixpoint over the finished listing's control-flow graph, tracking physical registers and the flags, computed after selection and allocation.

Wanted by: qaq.15 (lea where flags are dead), qaq.18 (dead materialisation in nbody's loop header, needs the back edge), qaq.26 (two dead stores in fannkuch's hottest block).
design: Runs on the finished listing, after partition-into-functions, where blocks and edges are both visible. Backward fixpoint over the CFG; live-out of a block is the union of live-in of its successors. Physical registers, not vregs -- the whole point is to see what allocation created. Flags are one more element in the same lattice. Consumers ask 'is r dead at this point', which replaces peephole's dead-from? at the barrier case only; the intra-block scan stays as it is.
acceptance_criteria: The analysis exists with its own tests, including a not-inert assertion validated by breaking the pass (D133/D146 convention). At least one of qaq.15/18/26 is then closed by it with its instruction count falling and both oracles passing. Per D120 do NOT expect a speedup: all three payoffs are instructions, measured not to convert to time on either benchmark.
notes:
D177 RECOMMENDS CLOSING THIS RATHER THAN BUILDING IT. The three beads it would
unblock (qaq.15, qaq.18, qaq.26) have a combined measured payoff of zero wall
clock: D120 audited them, and D167 then tested the strongest counter-argument --
that a register copy is not a branch, so removing copies should relieve D112's
front-end stall -- by removing 9.9% of fannkuch's instructions and 2.9% of
nbody's. Neither clock moved.

Against that, this is a dataflow analysis over the finished listing carrying real
wrong-code risk: liveness wrong in the optimistic direction deletes a live
definition, and the peephole barrier it would relax exists because D99 and D100
were two such bugs.

Scope reduction is Nathan's call, so this is a recommendation and not a closure.
close_reason: Recommended for closing since D177 and measured since. Would be a dataflow analysis over the finished listing carrying real wrong-code risk -- liveness wrong in the optimistic direction deletes a live definition, and the peephole barrier it would relax exists because D99 and D100 were two such bugs. It unblocks qaq.15, qaq.18 and qaq.26, whose COMBINED measured payoff is zero wall clock: D120 audited them, and D167 then tested the strongest counter-argument by removing 9.9% of fannkuch's instructions and 2.9% of nbody's, and neither clock moved. Reopen if the analysis is ever wanted for a reason that pays; the three beads it unblocks come along free.

title: Three dead constant stores in fannkuch's hottest block
description: D101: count-flips.loop opens with 'mov $0x0,%rcx' which reads as dead -- rcx is overwritten before the call and unread on the other path -- but callconv-x86-64 returns values in (rax rcx rdx) for both tagged and raw-word, so rcx is live at every ret and no liveness-based pass may remove it. The function returns one value. Determine whether liveness at a ret can reflect the function's actual return arity rather than the convention's ceiling of three, and whether anything downstream (gcmeta's two-bit scratch-live field is mentioned in callconv.ss as the reason the ceiling is three) depends on all three being written. NOT yet established that this instruction is removable -- that is the question, not the premise.
acceptance_criteria: Either liveness at ret is narrowed to the return arity and the dead materialisations disappear, with fannkuch's deterministic instruction count falling against 27,033,942,394 and both oracles passing; or the reason all three must stay live is recorded and this closes. Do not remove a write without establishing that no caller and no GC metadata reads it.
notes:
D161 ANSWERS THIS. Two halves, neither as filed.

DCE is right to keep them: at vreg level (const t.216 raw-word 0) feeds
(cmp-eq t.219 ... k%7.217 t.216). Nothing is dead there. The redundancy is
CREATED later when the back end folds the constant into the compare as an
immediate (cmp $0x0,%rdx) and leaves the materialisation behind.

The peephole cannot remove it: drop-dead-copies is the right pass and mov is in
pure-moves, so the shape matches. It fails dead-from?, which stops at the
block-ending branch and answers #f for any non-scratch register. The store IS
dead on both successors -- ret path reads rax from r13, loop path overwrites rcx
before reading -- but proving that needs the successors, and this pass by
construction does not look at them. That conservatism came from D99/D100, two
wrong-code bugs caused by a scan running past a barrier. It stays.

Count is TWO now, not three: elision+merge took one with nobody aiming at it.

Blocked on the same missing analysis as qaq.15 and qaq.18: liveness over the
finished listing, across blocks. Not worth building for a payoff D120 measured
as instructions that do not convert to time.

PRIOR NOTES (replaced by a --notes instead of --append-notes; restored in
summary, full text is in docs/LEDGER.md):
- D109 refuted the filing premise. rcx is NOT live at every ret because of the
  (rax rcx rdx) return convention; transfer-uses gives (ret v) exactly the one
  vreg it returns, so liveness there is already precise.
- D120 value-case audit: payoff is measured in INSTRUCTIONS, which do not
  convert to time on either benchmark (D89, D111, D112).
- Back edge ruled out: it targets count-flips.loop's first instruction, not the
  prologue, so D97 retargeting works and nothing re-runs per iteration.

D164: the acceptance criterion above cites 27,033,942,394 as fannkuch's
instruction count to fall against. THAT BASELINE IS STALE. It is 29,877,604,024
now -- up 10.5% because unrolling went default-off (qaq.30), which bought 6.0% of
cycles. c-native is unchanged to the digit, so the move is ours and real, not
harness drift. Measure against the new figure.

D199 RE-VALIDATION after D167 reallocated this function. Claim holds, registers
moved, count confirmed at TWO (D161's correction of D109's three).

Current count-flips.loop:
  401677  mov  %rcx,%r10        loop variable copied in
  40167a  mov  $0x0,%rcx        <- DEAD: overwritten at 4016a7 before any read,
                                   and the ret path takes rax from r10
  ...
  L.else21:
  4016a7  mov  %r11,%rcx        overwrites it
  4016af  mov  $0x1,%r11        <- DEAD: r11 is redefined at 4016a4 next
                                   iteration and unread on the ret path
Registers are r10/r11 now, not r13/r14 as the earlier notes say.

WORTH NOTING WHAT D167 DID NOT DO HERE. It removed both copy-ins from
loop%2.224.loop, and removed none from this block -- count-flips still opens with
mov %rcx,%r10 and closes with mov %rdx,%rcx. D163's table already showed it: 6
register-to-register moves before and 6 after. The parameter is pinned to rcx and
the back edge writes rcx, so rcx is live across the body and the body cannot have
it. Live-range-scoped precoloring helps where the parameter DIES early; here it
does not die.
close_reason: Blocked on qaq.33, closed as not worth building. Re-validated in D200: TWO dead stores, not the three this bead was filed with (D109 miscounted, D161 corrected), at r10/r11 rather than the r13/r14 the notes name. D201 explains the copies that remain and why one of them is forced -- rcx is both the raw-word parameter register and the first argument register.

title: Implement callee-saved registers; the convention declares them and codegen ignores them
description: D95: there are ZERO push/pop instructions in the fannkuch and nbody binaries. callconv.ss defines callee-saved?, callconv-callee-saved and a header explaining the set is deliberately a subset of the host ABI's so values survive a foreign call, but no prologue saves a register and no epilogue restores one. No register survives a call by convention -- only by the callee happening not to write it. The whole-program clobber analysis is strictly more precise than a save/restore convention and costs nothing at leaves, but it has a floor a convention does not: as clobber sets union up the call graph the survivors thin out, and there is no way to say 'this one is mine whatever you do'. Measured consequence: the raw pool is 8 registers, both of count-flips' callees write 5 of them, so only r11/r13/r14 survive any call and the fannkuch flip counter is spilled to the stack and incremented there with a read-modify-write per iteration.
acceptance_criteria: A function using a designated callee-saved register saves it in its prologue and restores it in its epilogue; the clobber analysis excludes saved registers from what a call destroys; count-flips.loop keeps its counter in a register with no rsp read-modify-write; fannkuch's INSTRUCTION count (deterministic per D94) falls against 27,847,0xx,xxx; leaf functions gain no prologue they do not need; the SPEC.md and eleven-way bit-exact oracles both still pass; suite stays green.
notes:
D102 weakens the premise. This bead was justified by D95's reading that the flip counter spills ACROSS a call. It does not -- it crosses the call in r13 and what spills is the increment's result. And callee-saved registers would add no survivors here: the clobber analysis already establishes that neither callee writes r11, r13 or r14, so three raw registers survive every call without any convention. Declaring some callee-saved adds nothing the caller did not know. Kept open because the guarantee still matters for UNKNOWN callees and deep call graphs, where the analysis degrades -- but it is not the fannkuch win it was filed as. See qaq.27 for what actually appears wrong.
D120 VALUE-CASE AUDIT. This bead's payoff is measured in INSTRUCTIONS, and instruction count is measured NOT to convert to time on either benchmark: nbody's spare instructions are free (D89 -- 465M removed, 18M cycles slower), and on fannkuch removing 863M instructions and 861M branches cost 3.5% wall clock (D111) because 25.2% of its cycles are front-end stalled on mispredicts (D112). Nothing here is wrong and the work may still be worth doing for code quality, but it should not be scheduled expecting a speedup. The two beads that target a measured bottleneck are qaq.29 (merging the duplicated reversal functions removes branch TARGETS, which is what the front end is stalling on) and qaq.30 (same mechanism, already measured at 5.6%).

D162 REPLACES THE JUSTIFICATION. D95's premise died with D102; this is the real
mechanism, and it is measured.

callee-first emits any call-graph CYCLE with NO clobber information, so every
call to a member assumes the entire register file is destroyed. Instrumented:
  fannkuch  6 of 14 unresolved: (main.entry1 join.133 join.129 next step main)
  nbody     no cycle at all -- the analysis is complete there

Static consequence, rsp-relative moves per function:
  next.loop 12, step.loop 9, count-flips.loop 0
ALL the spill traffic in the program is in two functions and both are cycle
members. The hottest block has none (D102 holding). Callee-saved registers fix
exactly this: a guaranteed survivor set independent of what the analysis can
prove.

BEFORE SCHEDULING, measure whether it converts to time. 21 is a static
instruction count and D120 says counts do not convert on fannkuch. A spill is a
load plus a store rather than an ALU op, so D89/D111 do not transfer
automatically -- but neither does the opposite. Run MODE=record
harness/vm-perf.sh on fannkuch and check next.loop's share of samples. If
next.loop is cold, close this bead; nbody needs nothing here either way.

D163 MEASURES THE CEILING. next.loop is 9.36% of the profile and step.loop 1.11%
-- 10.47% between them, and next.loop is only fifth. NONE of the four hottest
blocks (77.5% of the profile) spills at all. The spill traffic is real and still
confined to the two cycle members, but this is a 10% target, not a hot-path one,
and qaq.21 is roughly seven times the opportunity. Stays P4.

D177: THIS BEAD MAY BE ASKING FOR THE WRONG FIX. It wants callee-saved registers
so values survive calls into the unresolved functions. But D162 found why they are
unresolved: callee-first has no order for a call-graph CYCLE, so every member is
emitted with no clobber information at all. That -- not the absence of a
convention -- is what spills 21 values in next.loop and step.loop.

A fixpoint over the cycle is the smaller fix and it is NOT obviously sound: a
clobber set is physical registers and so exists only after allocation, while
allocation consumes clobber sets. Re-allocating a member with better information
changes what it writes, invalidating what the other members were just allocated
against. Show it monotone, or bound it with a verified fallback to the pessimistic
answer. Do not assume convergence.

Payoff either way is D163's 10.47% of the profile, on a benchmark where this
project has now measured instruction-level wins converting to nothing three times
(D89, D111, D167).

D178 CLOSES THE SOUNDNESS QUESTION D177 RAISED. The fixpoint is safe if it
verifies rather than assumes:
  round 1  allocate cycle members with clobbers=#f (today's behaviour) -> C1
  round 2  assume A(f)=C1(f), allocate again -> C2
  accept   round 2 iff C2(f) subset-of A(f) for EVERY member, else keep round 1
A caller allocated against A is correct iff its callee writes C subset-of A, which
is the existing contract -- that is why #f meaning 'assume everything' is sound.
Non-monotonicity stops mattering because it is DETECTED, not reasoned around.
Discard whole rounds: a mixture of two assignments is the bug being avoided.

Cost: one extra allocation of cycle members only (6 of fannkuch's 14, none of
nbody's). Still does not establish the payoff is real -- that is D163's 10.47% on
a benchmark where D89, D111 and D167 all found instruction wins buying no time.

D179 MEASURES THE CEILING: 13 spill instructions, not 21.

Forced clobbers-of to answer '() for cycle members -- unsound to execute, exact to
count, and unbeatable by any real analysis since a real clobber set is never empty:
  next.loop 12 -> 5, step.loop 9 -> 3, total 21 -> 8
So 38% of the spill traffic is genuine register pressure that better clobber
information cannot touch, and D178's sound fixpoint (actual writes, not the empty
set) gets strictly less than 13.

RECOMMEND CLOSING. The mechanism is right and the repair is sound; the payoff is
bounded above by 13 instructions in functions worth 10.47% of the profile, on a
benchmark where D89, D111 and D167 all measured instruction wins buying no time --
the last one built specifically to break that pattern. Scope call is Nathan's.
close_reason: Ceiling measured in D179 and it is thirteen instructions, not twenty-one. Forcing clobbers-of to '() for cycle members -- unsound to execute, exact to count, unbeatable by any real analysis -- drops next.loop 12->5 and step.loop 9->3, so 38% of that spill traffic is genuine register pressure no clobber information can touch. Those functions are 10.47% of the profile (D163). D178 makes the repair sound if anyone wants it: verify C2 subset-of A rather than assume convergence.

title: A dead constant materialisation survives in the nbody loop header
description: D88: the inner loop opens 'mov $0x5,%rdi' at 401c0a, then 'cmp $0x5,%rsi' folds the same constant as an immediate, then 'imul $0x3,%rcx,%rdi' redefines rdi without reading it. The loop-exit block never reads rdi either, so the definition is dead on both paths -- one wasted instruction per iteration, ~50M at N=5e6. peephole.ss already has a rule for this shape (its tests assert 'a constant used TWICE folds into both, and the mov still goes'), and dce.ss removes dead const definitions by a whole-program criterion, so the question is which condition this particular loop fails. Suspect the back edge: a vreg defined in the loop header and redefined in the body may read as live across the edge.
acceptance_criteria: The dead materialisation no longer appears in the emitted nbody inner loop; instructions measured by harness/vm-perf.sh fall against D88's 3,321,837,373 baseline; whichever pass is extended keeps its existing tests green and gains one pinning this shape; suite stays green.
notes:
D89 downgrades this: instructions are measured to be free on this loop (we removed 465M and got SLOWER). The dead materialisation costs ~50M instructions and therefore approximately no cycles. Keep it as cleanliness/correctness of the peephole, not as a performance item.
D120 VALUE-CASE AUDIT. This bead's payoff is measured in INSTRUCTIONS, and instruction count is measured NOT to convert to time on either benchmark: nbody's spare instructions are free (D89 -- 465M removed, 18M cycles slower), and on fannkuch removing 863M instructions and 861M branches cost 3.5% wall clock (D111) because 25.2% of its cycles are front-end stalled on mispredicts (D112). Nothing here is wrong and the work may still be worth doing for code quality, but it should not be scheduled expecting a speedup. The two beads that target a measured bottleneck are qaq.29 (merging the duplicated reversal functions removes branch TARGETS, which is what the front end is stalling on) and qaq.30 (same mechanism, already measured at 5.6%).
D143 staleness check: the claim HOLDS. nbody's inner loop still opens 'mov %rdx,%rsi / mov $0x5,%rdi / cmp $0x5,%rsi', with rdi overwritten before any read -- two immediate materialisations in the block, at least one dead. gconst (D88) changed how the constant arrives (an immediate rather than a global load) and merge (D121) renamed the function from inner%24.4.385 to inner%24.197, but the dead store survives both. D110's two mechanisms still explain it.
D159 staleness check, after the check-elision thread (D153-D158): the claim STILL HOLDS. nbody's inner loop, now named inner%24.158, still opens 'mov %rdx,%rsi / mov $0x5,%rdi / cmp $0x5,%rsi' with rdi overwritten before any read. Raising ascent-rounds to 16 and turning unrolling off changed the function name and the surrounding code and did not touch this. D110's two mechanisms still explain it: a chk names an operand the emitted check does not read, and a folded constant at the end of a run keeps its materialisation.
D161: shares a root with qaq.15 and qaq.26. Same missing analysis -- cross-block liveness over the finished listing. The nbody case needs it across the BACK EDGE specifically, which the bead's original 'suspect the back edge' guess got right for the wrong reason: the pass does not mishandle the edge, it never looks past the block at all (dead-from? answers #f at any branch for a non-scratch register).

D199 RE-VALIDATION against the tree after D167. The claim HOLDS and its details
have changed; the description above names a register that is no longer the one.

Current inner%24.158.loop:
  401824  mov   $0x5,%rsi        <- defines rsi
  40182b  cmp   $0x5,%rdx        <- folds the same constant, does not read rsi
  40182f  jl / jmp
  L.then144:
  40183a  imul  $0x3,%rcx,%rsi   <- REDEFINES rsi without reading it
  L.else145:
  40190e  mov   %r15,%rbx / mov %rbx,%rax / add / ret   <- rsi unread

So the materialisation is still dead on both paths. Two things moved:
  - the register is rsi now, not rdi (D167 reallocated)
  - the 'mov %rdx,%rsi' copy D143 recorded at the loop head is GONE -- that was
    the copy-in D167's live-range-scoped precoloring removed

Still blocked on qaq.33, and D161's diagnosis is unchanged: dead-from? stops at
the block-ending branch and answers #f for any non-scratch register, so the
peephole cannot see that both successors leave rsi dead.
close_reason: Blocked on qaq.33, closed as not worth building. Claim re-validated against the tree in D199 and it HOLDS -- mov $0x5,%rsi at 401824 is dead on both successors. Note the register is rsi now, not the rdi this bead names; D167 reallocated the function and also removed the mov %rdx,%rsi copy that used to open the block. D161 has the diagnosis: dead-from? stops at the block-ending branch and answers #f for any non-scratch register.

title: EFLAGS liveness, to make lea legal where flags are dead
description: target-x86-64.ss spells three-address add as mov+add, and D84 reverted an imul->lea strength reduction, both for one reason: lea sets no flags and an overflow chk reads whatever the preceding arithmetic left. A liveness analysis on EFLAGS over the machine listing would make both legal wherever no check consumes them. Measured payoff on nbody: 22 imuls (none followed by jo) and 6 collapsible mov+add pairs out of 56 adds, in a 1525-instruction binary. Real but small -- filed so the reasoning is not re-derived, not scheduled.
acceptance_criteria: A pass computes EFLAGS liveness over the machine listing; lea substitution fires only where flags are dead at the definition point; the existing peephole tests that pin imul are updated ONLY for cases proven flag-dead, with the proof stated; suite stays at 8572/0/58.
notes:
D120 VALUE-CASE AUDIT. This bead's payoff is measured in INSTRUCTIONS, and instruction count is measured NOT to convert to time on either benchmark: nbody's spare instructions are free (D89 -- 465M removed, 18M cycles slower), and on fannkuch removing 863M instructions and 861M branches cost 3.5% wall clock (D111) because 25.2% of its cycles are front-end stalled on mispredicts (D112). Nothing here is wrong and the work may still be worth doing for code quality, but it should not be scheduled expecting a speedup. The two beads that target a measured bottleneck are qaq.29 (merging the duplicated reversal functions removes branch TARGETS, which is what the front end is stalling on) and qaq.30 (same mechanism, already measured at 5.6%).
D161: shares a root with qaq.18 and qaq.26. All three are blocked on the same missing analysis -- liveness over the FINISHED listing (registers and flags), computed across blocks rather than within one. None justifies building it alone; if it is ever built for a reason that pays, all three come along free.
close_reason: Blocked on qaq.33, which is closed as not worth building. Premise still stands and is structural: lea sets no flags, so it is illegal where flags are live (D84 found that the hard way -- imul->lea is a wrong-code bug because overflow checks read the flags). Nothing here is wrong; the payoff is instructions on benchmarks where D89, D111 and D167 each measured instructions buying no time.
